details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Transmural myocardial ischemia/necrosis caused by complete, acute thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery following vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque rupture.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Plaque rupture exposes subendothelial collagen, causing platelet activation, aggregation, and fibrin clot formation, completely occluding coronary blood flow and producing ischemic cell death.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Severe, crushing retrosternal chest pain radiating to left arm/jaw, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, anxiety, S4 gallop, hypotension/shock in massive MI.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: ST-segment elevation >= 1 mm in >= 2 contiguous leads (or new LBBB); elevated high-sensitivity Cardiac Troponin I/T; emergency Primary PCI (< 90 mins) or Thrombolysis (< 12 hrs if PCI unavailable); MONAC (Morphine, Oxygen, Nitrates, Aspirin 300mg, Clopidogrel/Ticagrelor).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Subendocardial myocardial necrosis resulting from subtotal or transient coronary arterial occlusion without persistent ST-segment elevation.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Partial thrombotic occlusion or severe demand supply mismatch leads to ischemia confined to the subendocardium, causing cellular death and cardiac biomarker release.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Anginal chest pain at rest or minimal exertion, radiating to jaw/arm, diaphoresis, shortness of breath, autonomic symptoms.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Elevated Troponin I/T (serial testing at 0 and 1-3 hrs); ECG shows ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, or normal ECG; dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor), LMWH/Fondaparinux, early invasive risk-stratified coronary angiography.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Myocardial ischemia at rest or with minimal exertion without detectable myocardial necrosis or enzyme release.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Transient coronary arterial plaque instability or vasospasm causing temporary ischemia without permanent cardiomyocyte death.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: New-onset severe angina, crescendo angina (increasing frequency/intensity), or angina at rest lasting > 20 mins; relieved poorly by rest/nitrates.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Normal cardiac Troponin levels (distinguishes UA from NSTEMI); transient ST depression or T wave inversion on ECG; Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, LMWH, beta-blockers, anti-ischemic therapy, risk stratification.

Final Part 2 - Cardiology Database.Name: Acute Heart Failure & Acute Pulmonary Edema

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Rapid onset or worsening of heart failure symptoms requiring urgent medical evaluation and resuscitation; high acute mortality.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Sudden elevation in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) causes acute back-pressure into pulmonary capillaries, driving fluid transudation into alveoli and severely impairing gas exchange.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Severe acute dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), pink frothy sputum, diaphoresis, bilateral pulmonary crackles/rales, S3 gallop, elevated JVP.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Elevated BNP / NT-proBNP; CXR showing cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, Kerley B lines, bat-wing shadowing; LMNOP protocol: Loop diuretics (IV Furosemide), Morphine (for anxiety/preload reduction), Nitrates (IV/SL if SBP >= 100 mmHg), Oxygen/NIV, Position upright.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Complex clinical syndrome characterized by structural/functional cardiac impairment resulting in inadequate cardiac output or elevated intracardiac pressures.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: HFrEF (LVEF <= 40%): impaired myocardial contractility (post-MI, dilated cardiomyopathy). HFpEF (LVEF >= 50%): impaired diastolic relaxation and compliance (hypertension, LVH). Neurohormonal activation (RAAS, SNS) drives adverse ventricular remodeling.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Exertional dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, PND, peripheral edema, elevated JVP, displaced apex beat, S3 (HFrEF) or S4 (HFpEF) gallop, hepatomegaly.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Echocardiogram (LVEF measurement); elevated BNP/NT-proBNP; NYHA functional class I-IV grading; HFrEF disease-modifying therapy: ACEi/ARNI, Beta-blockers (Bisoprolol/Carvedilol), MRA (Spironolactone/Eplerenone), SGLT2 inhibitors.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Systemic immune-mediated inflammatory sequela occurring 2-4 weeks following Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis; predominantly affects children/young adults in developing regions.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M-protein and human cardiac tissue epitopes leads to cross-reactive antibody and T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium (pancarditis).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Major Jones Criteria: Carditis, Polyarthritis (migratory), Sydenham Chorea, Erythema Marginatum, Subcutaneous Nodules. Chronic RHD leads to progressive valve deformity (Mitral Stenosis > Mitral Regurgitation > Aortic valve disease).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Revised Jones Criteria (2 Major OR 1 Major + 2 Minor plus evidence of preceding GABHS infection: elevated ASO titer or positive throat swab/culture); anti-inflammatory therapy (Aspirin/corticosteroids); long-term secondary penicillin prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G every 3-4 weeks).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Narrowing of the mitral valve orifice, almost exclusively secondary to chronic Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Restricted mitral leaflet mobility and fusion of commissures obstruct left atrial emptying into LV, leading to elevated LA pressure, LA enlargement (atrial fibrillation, thrombus formation), and secondary pulmonary arterial hypertension.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, hemoptysis (bronchial vein rupture), malar flush (pink-purple patches on cheeks), systemic embolic events (stroke), signs of RV failure in late stages.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Auscultation: Loud S1, opening snap (OS) following S2, low-pitched mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at apex heard best in left lateral decubitus position; Echocardiogram (planimetry, pressure half-time, Wilkins score); Percutaneous Mitral Balloon Commissurotomy (PMBC) or valve replacement.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, most commonly affecting native or prosthetic heart valves; Staphylococcus aureus (acute/IVDU) and Streptococcus viridans (subacute/dental procedures).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Bacteremia leads to bacterial adherence on pre-existing sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations or damaged valvular endothelium, causing progressive valve destruction, regurgitation, abscess formation, and septic embolization.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Fever, night sweats, weight loss, new or changing heart murmur, peripheral vascular/immunologic stigmata: Janeway lesions (painless erythematous macules on palms/soles), Osler nodes (painful subcutaneous nodules on digits), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages), splinter hemorrhages.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Modified Duke Criteria (Major: >=2 positive blood cultures for typical organisms, Echocardiogram showing vegetation/abscess/dehiscence; Minor: predisposing heart condition/IVDU, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena); prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics (4-6 weeks); surgical intervention if severe valve failure or persistent bacteremia.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Severe acute elevation of blood pressure (typically SBP > 180 mmHg or DBP > 120 mmHg). Differentiated strictly by the presence of acute target organ damage.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Failure of vascular autoregulation under severe pressure load causes endothelial injury, fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, intravascular coagulation, and acute target organ ischemia.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Hypertensive Urgency: severe headache, epistaxis, anxiety, but NO acute organ damage. Hypertensive Emergency: BP > 180/120 with acute encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute coronary syndrome, acute pulmonary edema, eclampsia, or AKI.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Fundoscopy (papilledema, flame hemorrhages, soft exudates); serum creatinine, urinalysis, CT head, ECG, CXR. Urgency: oral antihypertensives (Labetalol, Captopril) over 24-48 hrs. Emergency: ICU admission, IV labetalol/nicardipine/sodium nitroprusside (reduce MAP by <= 25% in 1st hour).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Sustained elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure (SBP >= 140 mmHg or DBP >= 90 mmHg) without an identifiable secondary cause; accounts for 90-95% of adult hypertension cases.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Multifactorial interplay of genetic susceptibility, excessive sodium intake, sympathetic nervous system overactivity, RAAS dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and decreased endothelial nitric oxide availability.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Usually asymptomatic ('silent killer'); long-term unmanaged HTN leads to target organ damage: LV hypertrophy, coronary artery disease, stroke, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, retinopathy.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Repeated BP measurements or 24-hr Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM average >= 130/80 mmHg); screening for target organ damage (ECG for LVH, urinalysis for microalbuminuria, U&Es); 1st line pharmacological management: ACEi/ARB, Calcium Channel Blockers (Amlodipine), Thiazide-like diuretics (Indapamide).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute poisoning from agricultural organophosphate/carbamate pesticides; high mortality via oral ingestion, inhalation, or dermal absorption.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) enzyme, causing acetylcholine accumulation at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: DUMBBELSS (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation, Sweating); fasciculations, paralysis, seizures, coma.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Red blood cell / serum cholinesterase activity (<20-50%); Atropine stat (1.8-3 mg IV double q3-5m until clear chest lungs/dry secretions) + Pralidoxime (oxime).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute toxic hepatopathy caused by intentional or accidental ingestion of >7.5-10 g (or >150 mg/kg) paracetamol.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Excess N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) toxic metabolite depletes hepatic glutathione, causing hepatocellular necrosis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Phase 1: Nausea/vomiting. Phase 2 (24-48h): RUQ pain, elevated AST/ALT. Phase 3 (72-96h): Jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, AKI, liver failure.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Serum paracetamol level plotted on Rumack-Matthew nomogram; elevated AST/ALT/INR; N-acetylcysteine (NAC) IV/oral stat (most effective within 8 hours).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute toxicity from heroin, morphine, methadone, fentanyl, or codeine ingestion/injection.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Overstimulation of mu-opioid receptors in CNS depresses brainstem respiratory center and blunts responsiveness to hypercapnia/hypoxia.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Opioid triad: CNS depression/coma, pin-point pupils (miosis), and severe respiratory depression/apnea; hypothermia, bradycardia, pulmonary edema.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Clinical diagnosis; urine toxicology screen; ABG showing respiratory acidosis; immediate bag-valve-mask ventilation + IV/IM Naloxone (0.4-2 mg stat).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Envenomation by Russell's viper or Saw-scaled viper; primary toxicity is hemotoxic and vasculotoxic.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Procoagulant toxins activate clotting factors causing consumption coagulopathy (DIC-like state), microvascular damage, and local tissue necrosis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Severe local swelling, blistering, active bleeding from bite site, gums, hematuria, hemoptysis, hypovolemic/septic shock, acute kidney injury.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: 20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT) showing uncoagulable blood; polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) 10 vials IV in 0.9% NS over 1 hour.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Envenomation by Naja naja (Cobra) or Bungarus caeruleus (Krait); nocturnal bites frequently while sleeping.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Post-synaptic (Cobra) or pre-synaptic (Krait) neurotoxins block neuromuscular transmission at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Bilateral ptosis, diplopia, ophthalmoplegia, dysphagia, dysarthria, descending flaccid paralysis, respiratory muscle paralysis/apnea.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Neurological clinical signs; 20WBCT (usually normal); polyvalent ASV 10 vials IV + Neostigmine (0.5-2.5 mg IV) + Atropine (for post-synaptic neurotoxicity).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Life-threatening hyperthermic emergency defined by core body temperature >40°C (104°F) accompanied by severe CNS dysfunction.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Failure of thermoregulation leads to systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), cellular protein denaturation, multiorgan failure, and DIC.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Hyperpyrexia (>40°C), altered mental status, confusion, delirium, seizures, coma, hot dry skin (classic) or diaphoresis (exertional), hypotension.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Core (rectal) temperature >40°C; DIC panel, elevated CPK/renal function; immediate aggressive cooling (cold water immersion / evaporative mist + fan) to <38.5°C.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Severe, systemic, life-threatening Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction triggered by drugs (penicillins, NSAIDs), stings, or food.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Massive IgE-mediated degranulation of mast cells and basophils releases histamine, leukotrienes, and tryptase, causing systemic vasodilation and bronchospasm.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Urticaria, angioedema (lip/tongue/airway swelling), stridor, severe wheezing, profound hypotension, dizziness, collapse, abdominal cramps.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Clinical diagnosis; serum tryptase (retrospective); immediate Intramuscular Epinephrine / Adrenaline (1:1000, 0.5 mg IM anterolateral thigh stat, repeat q5-15m).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Severe ethanol ingestion coupled with chronic thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency common in alcohol use disorder.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Thiamine deficiency impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase, causing impaired cerebral glucose metabolism and oxidative neuronal damage in mammillary bodies.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Wernicke triad: Acute confusion/delirium, ataxia (broad-based gait), and ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus; hypoglycemia, stupor, hypothermia.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Bedside capillary blood glucose; clinical triad; High-dose IV Thiamine (500 mg IV TID x 3 days) ALWAYS administered BEFORE IV Dextrose infusion.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Thermal, chemical, or electrical injury involving deep partial-thickness or full-thickness destruction of skin surface area.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Massive systemic capillary leak driven by inflammatory cytokines leads to rapid fluid extravasation into interstitial space and burn shock.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Erythema, blistering, charred eschar, hypovolemic shock, oliguria, airway edema/stridor (inhalation injury), circumferential eschar constriction.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Percentage Total Body Surface Area (%TBSA) via Rule of Nines; Parkland Formula (4 mL x kg x %TBSA Ringer's Lactate in first 24h: 1/2 in first 8h).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Inhalation toxicity from incomplete combustion of carbonaceous fuels (generators, fires, faulty heaters) in enclosed spaces.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: CO binds hemoglobin with >200x affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb), shifting O2-Hb dissociation curve left and inhibiting cellular respiration.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Headache (most common early sign), dizziness, confusion, nausea, cherry-red skin (rare/late), angina, coma, seizures.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Arterial/venous blood gas co-oximetry showing elevated Carboxyhemoglobin (COHb >10-15%); 100% High-Flow Normobaric or Hyperbaric Oxygen (HBO).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells; absolute insulin deficiency; strong HLA-DR3 / HLA-DR4 association; typical onset in children and young adults.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Loss of beta cells eliminates endogenously secreted insulin, preventing cellular glucose uptake via GLUT4 and removing inhibition on gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and lipolysis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, rapid weight loss, lethargy, ketoacidosis propensity, microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular complications.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Fasting Plasma Glucose >= 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL); Random Glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) + symptoms; HbA1c >= 6.5%; undetectable/low C-peptide; positive Anti-GAD, IA-2, or ICA autoantibodies.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Progressive combination of insulin resistance in peripheral tissues (skeletal muscle, liver, adipose) and relative insulin secretory defect; strongly linked to obesity and metabolic syndrome.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Insulin receptor signaling impairment reduces GLUT4 translocation; compensatory hyperinsulinemia initially maintains euglycemia until beta cell exhaustion occurs.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Insidious onset, acanthosis nigricans, central obesity, fatigue, frequent infections, microvascular and macrovascular complications, hyperosmolar hyperglycemic propensity.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Fasting Plasma Glucose >= 7.0 mmol/L; 2-hour OGTT >= 11.1 mmol/L; HbA1c >= 6.5%; preserved or elevated C-peptide; negative islet autoantibodies.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Life-threatening emergency predominantly in T1DM; triggered by infection (pneumonia, UTI), insulin omission, or new-onset diabetes; characterized by absolute insulin lack and excess counter-regulatory hormones.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Unopposed lipolysis releases free fatty acids into circulation, which undergo hepatic beta-oxidation into ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate), causing anion gap metabolic acidosis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, profound dehydration, Kussmaul (deep/acidotic) respirations, acetone (fruity) breath odor, hypotension, altered mental status/coma.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Random blood glucose >= 11 mmol/L (> 200-250 mg/dL); arterial/venous pH < 7.3; serum HCO3 < 15 mmol/L; elevated blood/urine ketones (>= 2+); high anion gap (> 12 mEq/L).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Severe metabolic emergency primarily in elderly T2DM patients; triggered by acute illness, infection, MI, stroke, or inadequate fluid intake; extreme dehydration and hyperosmolality.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Residual endogenous insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis, preventing DKA, but is insufficient to suppress hepatic glucose production, causing profound osmotic diuresis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Insidious onset over days to weeks, severe lethargy, confusion, focal neurological deficits, seizures, coma, extreme dehydration (dry mucous membranes, delayed turgor), high thrombotic risk.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Severe hyperglycemia (blood glucose > 30 mmol/L / > 600 mg/dL); serum osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg; arterial pH > 7.3; serum HCO3 > 15 mmol/L; absent or minimal ketonemia.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Plasma glucose level low enough to cause brain energy deprivation; caused by sulfonylureas, insulin overdose, missed meals, strenuous exercise, or renal impairment.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Neuroglycopenia impairs CNS function while falling glucose triggers autonomic (sympathetic) counter-regulatory release of epinephrine, glucagon, cortisol, and growth hormone.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Autonomic signs: diaphoresis, tremors, tachycardia, anxiety, hunger. Neuroglycopenic signs: confusion, dizziness, visual disturbances, seizures, coma.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Plasma glucose < 3.0-3.9 mmol/L (< 55-70 mg/dL); Whipple's triad (symptoms of hypoglycemia, documented low blood glucose, relief of symptoms upon glucose administration).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Most common cause of hyperthyroidism; autoimmune disorder with female predominance (8:1); linked to HLA-DR3 and HLA-B8.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor autoantibodies (TRAb / TSH-R-Ab) continuously bind to and activate TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells, stimulating unregulated T3/T4 synthesis and release.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Heat intolerance, weight loss despite increased appetite, palpitations, fine resting tremor, frequent bowel movements, diffuse smooth goiter with bruit, exophthalmos/pretibial myxedema.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Suppressed TSH (< 0.05 mIU/L); elevated Free T4 and Free T3; positive TRAb (TSH receptor antibodies); diffuse increased radionuclide uptake on iodine-131 scan.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Extreme, life-threatening hypermetabolic manifestation of thyrotoxicosis; triggered by trauma, infection, surgery, parturition, or abrupt discontinuation of antithyroid medications.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Massive, acute surge in free thyroid hormone availability combined with heightened target tissue sensitivity to catecholamines causes hyperadrenergic collapse.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Hyperpyrexia (fever > 38.5-40 C), severe tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, delirium, agitation, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, high-output heart failure, shock.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Markedly suppressed TSH with dramatically elevated Free T4/T3; clinical scoring via Burch-Wartofsky scale; leucocytosis; elevated liver function tests.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions; chronic autoimmune thyroiditis marked by lymphocytic infiltration and follicular destruction.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid gland parenchyma leads to reduced thyroid hormone synthesis, triggering compensatory increase in anterior pituitary TSH secretion via negative feedback.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Cold intolerance, weight gain, fatigue, constipation, dry skin, coarse hair, periorbital puffiness, voice hoarseness, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes, menorrhagia.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Elevated serum TSH (> 4.5-10 mIU/L); reduced Free T4; positive anti-thyroperoxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) autoantibodies; diffuse heterogeneous echo on ultrasound.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: End-stage, severe, life-threatening complication of uncorrected hypothyroidism; triggered by cold exposure, systemic infection, sedatives, stroke, or MI in hypothyroid patients.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Profound thyroid hormone deficit leads to failure of cell thermogenesis, generalized hypometabolism, cellular edema (mucopolysaccharide deposition), and cardiovascular depression.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Hypothermia (< 35 C), profound bradycardia, hypoventilation (hypercapnia), altered mental status/coma, hypotension, generalized non-pitting periorbital and pretibial edema.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Dramatically elevated TSH with undetectable or near-zero Free T4; arterial blood gas showing respiratory acidosis (high PaCO2, low PaO2); severe hyponatremia; hypoglycemia.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Post-viral inflammatory thyroid disorder; typically follows upper respiratory tract viral infection (Coxsackievirus, influenza, adenovirus); HLA-B35 association.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Viral-induced granulomatous inflammation damages thyroid follicles, releasing preformed stored colloid into circulation (transient thyrotoxicosis), followed by transient hypothyroidism.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Painful, tender thyroid goiter radiating to jaw or ears, fever, fatigue, transient thyrotoxic symptoms followed by self-limiting hypothyroid phase.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Markedly elevated ESR (> 50-100 mm/hr) and CRP; transient high Free T4 with suppressed TSH; low/suppressed radioiodine (I-131) uptake (< 1-2%).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: State of chronic hypercortisolism. Cushing's Disease refers specifically to ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma; ACTH-independent causes include adrenal adenomas and exogenous steroids.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Excess glucocorticoids bind to glucocorticoid receptors, stimulating gluconeogenesis, muscle catabolism, subcutaneous fat redistribution, mineralocorticoid cross-reactivity, and immune suppression.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Truncal obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, easy bruising, hirsutism.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Elevated 24-hr urinary free cortisol; unsuppressed cortisol after 1 mg Overnight Low-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (LDDST); High-Dose Dexamethasone test suppresses pituitary ACTH (Cushing's Disease).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Autonomous, unregulated excess secretion of aldosterone from adrenal cortex (solitary adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Aldosterone activates mineralocorticoid receptors in renal cortical collecting duct principal cells, upregulating ENaC channels and Na+/K+-ATPase, causing Na+ retention, volume expansion, and K+/H+ wasting.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Refractory hypertension, muscle weakness, cramps, fatigue, paresthesias, polyuria/polydipsia (due to hypokalemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus); absence of peripheral edema due to aldosterone escape.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Hypokalemia (< 3.5 mmol/L); elevated plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) with suppressed plasma renin activity (PRA); Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR) > 20-30; high urinary aldosterone after saline load.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's) involves autoimmune destruction of all adrenal cortical zones; Addisonian Crisis is an acute, life-threatening decompensation triggered by stress, infection, or trauma.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Deficiency of cortisol (impaired vascular tone and gluconeogenesis) and aldosterone (renal Na+ wasting and K+ retention); elevated POMC cleavage yields excess ACTH and MSH.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Addison's: fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension, hyperpigmentation (skin creases, buccal mucosa). Crisis: hypovolemic shock, severe abdominal pain, high fever, vomiting, confusion.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, elevated BUN/creatinine; morning cortisol < 3 ug/dL; unsuppressed plasma ACTH (> 100 pg/mL in primary); failed short Synacthen (cosyntropin) stimulation test.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Rare catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla (10% rule: 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, 10% malignant); associated with MEN2, VHL, NF1.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Episodic or continuous secretion of norepinephrine and epinephrine activates vascular alpha-1 receptors (intense vasoconstriction) and cardiac beta-1 receptors (positive inotropy/chronotropy).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Classic triad: paroxysmal severe headache, profuse diaphoresis, and tachycardia/palpitations; accompanied by paroxysmal or sustained severe hypertension, tremor, anxiety.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Elevated 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and normetanephrines; elevated plasma free metanephrines; CT/MRI abdomen demonstrating adrenal mass; MIBG scan for extra-adrenal localization.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Chronic hypersecretion of Growth Hormone (GH) occurring post-epiphyseal plate closure, almost exclusively caused by a somatotroph pituitary macroadenoma.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Excess pituitary GH stimulates hepatic synthesis and secretion of Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1), driving somatic growth, soft tissue proliferation, cartilage growth, and insulin resistance.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Enlargement of hands and feet (increased shoe/ring size), coarsening of facial features, prognathism, macroglossia, deep voice, carpel tunnel syndrome, bitemporal hemianopia, secondary diabetes.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Elevated serum IGF-1 (initial screening test of choice); failure to suppress serum GH to < 1 ug/L following a 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT); pituitary MRI demonstrating adenoma.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: First-line oral antidiabetic drug for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; non-hypoglycemic agent; weight-neutral or promotes modest weight loss.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), decreasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, increasing intestinal glucose absorption, and enhancing peripheral insulin sensitivity.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: First-line T2DM therapy; reduces cardiovascular risk; common side effects include GI upset (diarrhea, nausea, bloating) and Vitamin B12 deficiency; rare risk of lactic acidosis.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: eGFR monitoring required (contraindicated or dose-reduced if eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m2); periodic plasma Vitamin B12 levels and renal function testing.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Insulin secretagogue class of antidiabetic agents used in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Binds to and closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels (SUR1 subunit) on pancreatic beta cell membranes, causing cell depolarization, influx of voltage-gated calcium, and exocytosis of preformed insulin vesicles.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Used as second-line or dual therapy in T2DM; key adverse effects include hypoglycemia and weight gain; cautious use in elderly and renal impairment.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Requires blood glucose monitoring; serum creatinine/eGFR check (risk of prolonged drug accumulation in renal insufficiency).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Thionamide antithyroid medications used in hyperthyroidism, Graves' disease, and thyroid storm.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzyme, preventing oxidation of iodide, organification of iodine into tyrosine residues, and coupling of iodotyrosines (MIT/DIT). PTU also blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Used for medical management of Graves' disease and toxic nodular goiter; PTU preferred in 1st trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm; risk of agranulocytosis and PTU hepatotoxicity.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Serial TFTs (TSH, Free T4/T3); baseline and urgent Complete Blood Count (WBC count for agranulocytosis if fever/sore throat occurs); LFTs.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Synthetic form of thyroxine (T4); mainstay of hormone replacement therapy for hypothyroidism.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: Converted peripherally by deiodinase enzymes into active triiodothyronine (T3), which binds to nuclear thyroid hormone receptors to regulate gene expression, metabolic rate, and protein synthesis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Treatment of primary, secondary, and congenital hypothyroidism; myxedema coma (IV form); suppression therapy in thyroid carcinoma; adverse effects of overtreatment include atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Targeted monitoring via serum TSH (aiming for 0.5-2.5 mIU/L in primary hypothyroidism); Free T4 monitoring in central/secondary hypothyroidism.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Aqueous solution of elemental iodine and potassium iodide used in acute thyrotoxic crisis and pre-thyroidectomy preparation.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathogenesis
details.content: High concentration of inorganic iodide transiently inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and release via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect and decreases thyroid gland vascularity.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Associations
details.content: Administered in Thyroid Storm (always given at least 1 hour after antithyroid drug administration) and pre-operatively 10-14 days prior to thyroidectomy to reduce operative bleeding.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Lab Tests
details.content: Serum Free T4/T3 tracking; pulse rate and cardiac rhythm monitoring.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Mucosal erosion in stomach or duodenum (> 5 mm) extending into submucosa; primary causes are Helicobacter pylori infection (~85-90% duodenal, ~70-80% gastric) and NSAID/Aspirin use.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Disruption of mucosal defense mechanisms (bicarbonate barrier, prostaglandins) by H. pylori (cytotoxin-associated gene A/CagA, vacuolating cytotoxin/VacA) or NSAIDs (COX-1 inhibition reducing protective prostaglandins), leading to acid-peptic mucosal necrosis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Epigastric pain (duodenal: relieved by food/antacids, pain 2-3 hrs post-meal; gastric: aggravated by food, weight loss), postprandial fullness, early satiety. Red flags: hematemesis, melena, persistent vomiting, anemia, sudden acute abdomen (perforation).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: EGD (gold standard biopsy/ulcer visualization); H. pylori testing (urea breath test, stool antigen test, rapid urease biopsy test). Treatment: Triple therapy (PPI + Amoxicillin 1g BD + Clarithromycin 500mg BD for 14 days) or Bismuth quadruple therapy; stop NSAIDs.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Bleeding originating proximal to the ligament of Treitz; non-variceal (PUD, Mallory-Weiss tear, erosive gastritis, Dieulafoy lesion) vs. variceal (portal hypertension secondary to cirrhosis).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Erosion of mucosal arteries by acid-peptic ulceration or acute rupture of high-pressure submucosal esophageal/gastric varices secondary to portal venous hypertension.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Hematemesis ('coffee-ground' emesis or bright red blood), melena (black tarry stool), hematochezia (if massive rapid transit), postural hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, pallor, hypovolemic shock.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Immediate resuscitation: IV wide-bore access, IV 0.9% Normal Saline, blood transfusion (target Hb 7-8 g/dL). Variceal: IV Terlipressin/Octreotide + prophylactic IV Ceftriaxone + urgent EGD with Band Ligation (EVL) within 12h. Non-variceal: high-dose IV PPI drip + EGD dual therapy (adrenaline + clip/cautery).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute inflammatory disease of the pancreas; most common causes are gallstones (cholelithiasis ~40%) and heavy alcohol consumption (~30%); other causes include hypertriglyceridemia, ERCP, drugs, hypercalcemia.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Premature intra-acinar activation of zymogens (trypsinogen into trypsin), initiating autodigestion of pancreatic parenchyma, microvascular injury, fat necrosis, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and multiorgan dysfunction.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Severe, constant epigastric pain radiating directly to the back, relieved by leaning forward; nausea, vomiting, fever, paralytic ileus. Severe cases: Cullen sign (periumbilical ecchymosis), Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis), hypotension, ARDS.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Serum amylase and lipase >= 3x upper limit of normal (lipase more specific); abdominal ultrasound (gallstones); contrast-enhanced CT abdomen at 72h (necrosis/pseudocyst). Management: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (Ringer's lactate), analgesia, enteral nutrition, ERCP if cholangitis.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Progressive, irreversible inflammatory and fibrotic disease of the pancreas leading to loss of endocrine and exocrine function; chronic alcohol abuse (> 70-80%), hereditary, tropical, or idiopathic causes.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Repeated acute injury drives pancreatic stellate cell activation, dense acinar parenchyma fibrosis, ductal strictures, intraductal stone formation, and progressive irreversible destruction of acinar and islet cells.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Recurrent or persistent severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea, foul-smelling bulky floating stools, fat-soluble vitamin A/D/E/K deficiencies), endocrine insufficiency (pancreatogenic/type 3c diabetes mellitus), weight loss.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Fecal elastase-1 (< 200 ug/g indicates exocrine insufficiency); CT/MRI/EUS showing pancreatic calcifications, ductal dilation ('chain of lakes' pattern). Treatment: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT/Creon taken with meals), pain management, low-fat diet, insulin for diabetes.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Yellowish discoloration of skin and sclera due to serum total bilirubin > 35-50 umol/L (2-3 mg/dL); classified into pre-hepatic (unconjugated), hepatic (mixed), and post-hepatic/cholestatic (conjugated).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Pre-hepatic: excess heme breakdown (hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis). Hepatic: impaired hepatic uptake, conjugation (Gilbert/Crigler-Najjar), or hepatocellular secretion (hepatitis, cirrhosis). Post-hepatic: mechanical biliary tree obstruction (choledocholithiasis, pancreatic head carcinoma).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Scleral icterus, jaundice. Cholestatic hallmarks: dark tea-colored urine, pale/clay-colored stools, intense pruritus, xanthelasma. Red flags: fever + rigor + jaundice + RUQ pain (Charcot triad for acute cholangitis; add hypotension + confusion = Reynolds pentad).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: LFTs: Cholestatic pattern (marked ALP/GGT elevation > AST/ALT); Hepatocellular pattern (marked AST/ALT elevation > ALP). Abdominal ultrasound (biliary dilation); MRCP / ERCP for obstructive ductal lesions.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Rapid-onset severe liver injury in a patient WITHOUT pre-existing cirrhosis, characterized by coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy within 24 weeks of onset; paracetamol toxicity (most common), viral hepatitis (A, B, E), idiosyncratic drug reactions.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Massive hepatocyte necrosis causes acute loss of synthetic function (clotting factors, albumin), metabolic clearance failure (ammonia accumulation), systemic vasodilation, cerebral edema, hyperammonemia-mediated astrocyte swelling, and multiorgan failure.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy (Grade I: confusion/mood change; Grade II: lethargy/flapping tremor/asterixis; Grade III: stupor; Grade IV: coma), cerebral edema (increased ICP, sluggish pupils), mucosal bleeding, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Coagulopathy (INR > 1.5, prolonged PT); elevated serum ammonia, bilirubin, transaminases; arterial lactate; hypoglycemia. Management: ICU support, N-acetylcysteine (NAC for paracetamol and non-paracetamol ALF), Lactulose/Rifaximin, mannitol/3% hypertonic saline for cerebral edema; urgent liver transplant evaluation (King's College Criteria).

Final Part 2 - Gastroenterology & Hepato.Name: Viral Hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E)

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Systemic viral infection primarily targeting hepatocytes; HAV/HEV (fecal-oral, acute only except HEV in pregnancy/immunocompromised); HBV/HCV/HDV (parenteral/sexual/vertical transmission, risk of chronicity).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Immune-mediated hepatocyte destruction (cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell attack against viral antigens on hepatocytes) leading to lobular inflammation, ballooning degeneration, Councilman bodies (apoptotic hepatocytes), and potential chronic fibrosis/cirrhosis (HBV/HCV).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Prodrome: malaise, low-grade fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, RUQ discomfort; icteric phase: jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, hepatomegaly. Chronic HBV/HCV: often asymptomatic until cirrhosis, portal hypertension, or Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) develops.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Acute HAV/HEV: IgM anti-HAV / IgM anti-HEV. HBV serology panel: HBsAg (active infection), Anti-HBs (immunity), IgM Anti-HBc (acute infection), IgG Anti-HBc (past/chronic infection), HBeAg (high replicative state/infectivity), HBV DNA. HCV: Anti-HCV screening + HCV RNA PCR. Treatment: Nucleos(t)ide analogs (Tenofovir, Entecavir) for HBV; Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs like Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir) for HCV (> 95% cure).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: End-stage chronic liver disease defined histologically by diffuse hepatic fibrosis and conversion of normal architecture into structurally abnormal regenerative nodules; major causes: chronic alcohol abuse, chronic HBV/HCV, MASLD/MASH.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Disruption of hepatic architecture increases intrahepatic vascular resistance, causing portal venous pressure > 10-12 mmHg (portal hypertension), splanchnic vasodilation, arterial underfilling, RAAS/ADH activation, fluid retention (ascites), and portosystemic collateral formation.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Stigmata of chronic liver disease: spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, Dupuytren contracture, caput medusae. Complications: ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), esophageal variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome (HRS).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Serum albumin < 35 g/L, prolonged PT/INR, thrombocytopenia (splenomegaly/hypersplenism); liver USG (nodular surface, splenomegaly, ascites); transient elastography (FibroScan). Ascites paracentesis: SAAG >= 11 g/L indicates portal hypertension; neutrophil count >= 250/mm3 diagnoses SBP (treat with IV Cefotaxime/Ceftriaxone).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Diarrhea lasting > 4 weeks; malabsorption syndromes characterized by impaired nutrient absorption across intestinal mucosa. Key causes: Celiac Disease (autoimmune gluten sensitivity), Tropical Sprue, Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn's, Ulcerative Colitis), Chronic Pancreatitis.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Celiac: immune response against gliadin triggers villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis in duodenum/jejunum. Crohn's: transmural, skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas anywhere from mouth to anus. Ulcerative Colitis: continuous mucosal inflammation starting at rectum extending proximally.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Chronic watery/fatty stools (steatorrhea: bulky, pale, foul-smelling floating stools), weight loss, muscle wasting, anemia (iron deficiency in duodenal disease, B12/folate in ileal disease), metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia/osteoporosis due to vitamin D malabsorption), peripheral edema (hypoalbuminemia).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Celiac: anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) IgA + total IgA; duodenal biopsy (gold standard). IBD: fecal calprotectin (elevated), colonoscopy with biopsies (Crohn's: cobblestoning, linear ulcers, skip lesions; UC: continuous mucosal ulceration, pseudopolyps). Stool microscopy, fat quantification.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute infectious enteritis/colitis; Cholera (Vibrio cholerae, non-invasive secretory diarrhea); Bacillary Dysentery (Shigella spp.); Amoebic Dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: V. cholerae: cholera toxin increases mucosal intracellular cAMP, driving massive active secretion of Cl- and water into gut lumen. Shigella: Shiga toxin + mucosal invasion causing acute hemorrhagic colitis. E. histolytica: trophozoite tissue invasion forming characteristic 'flask-shaped' mucosal ulcers.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Cholera: painless, massive, profuse 'rice-water' watery diarrhea (up to 1L/hr), rapid severe dehydration, hypovolemic shock, sunken eyes, muscle cramps. Dysentery: painful frequent small-volume bloody mucoid stools, severe tenesmus, high fever (Shigella), or right lobe liver abscess (Amoebic).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Stool dark-field microscopy / culture (V. cholerae); stool microscopy for E. histolytica trophozoites containing ingested RBCs or Shigella WBCs/blood. Treatment: Cholera: aggressive oral rehydration solution (ORS) or IV Ringer's lactate + Doxycycline/Azithromycin; Amoebic: Metronidazole/Tinidazole followed by luminal agent (Diloxanide furoate or Paromomycin); Shigella: Ciprofloxacin or Azithromycin.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Most common cause of anemia worldwide; microcytic hypochromic; caused by chronic blood loss (GI bleeding, menorrhagia), poor dietary intake, malabsorption (Celiac), or increased demand (pregnancy).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Depletion of body iron stores leads to impaired heme synthesis, resulting in small, pale erythrocytes with reduced hemoglobin content and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Fatigue, pallor, weakness, dyspnea on exertion, pica (pagophagia - ice craving), koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), angular stomatitis, glossitis, dysphagia (Plummer-Vinson syndrome).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Low Hb, low MCV (< 80 fL), low MCH; low serum ferritin (most specific test, < 30 ug/L), high TIBC, low serum iron, low transferrin saturation; Management: Oral Ferrous Sulfate (200 mg tid) with Vitamin C, treat underlying cause.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Inherited autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathy; Beta-thalassemia major (Cooley anemia) caused by beta-globin gene mutations; Alpha-thalassemia caused by alpha-globin gene deletions.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Imbalance in globin chain synthesis leads to precipitation of unpaired globin chains, causing intramedullary hemolysis (ineffective erythropoiesis) and peripheral hemolysis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Severe anemia starting in infancy, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, frontal bossing and maxillary reexpansion ('chipmunk' facies, crew-cut skull on X-ray), iron overload (hemochromatosis).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Microcytic target cells, basophilic stippling; Hb electrophoresis showing elevated HbF and HbA2 in Beta-thalassemia major; Management: Regular blood transfusions with iron chelation therapy (Deferasirox/Deferoxamine), splenectomy.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Macrocytic anemia caused by Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency (Pernicious anemia - anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, ileal resection) or Folate deficiency (poor diet, alcoholism, antifolate drugs like MTX).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Impaired DNA synthesis disrupts nuclear maturation while cytoplasmic development proceeds normally, leading to megaloblastic erythroblasts, hypersegmented neutrophils, and ineffective hematopoiesis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Anemia symptoms, lemon-yellow skin jaundice, smooth beefy red tongue (glossitis). B12 specific: Subacute Combined Degeneration of Spinal Cord (loss of vibration/position sense, spastic paraparesis).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: High MCV (> 100-110 fL), hypersegmented neutrophils (>= 5 lobes) on blood film; low serum B12 or serum folate; anti-IF/anti-parietal cell antibodies; Management: IM Hydroxocobalamin for B12; oral Folic Acid (5 mg daily) AFTER B12 rule-in.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Hemolytic anemias divided into immune-mediated (Warm IgG vs Cold IgM Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia) and enzymopathies (X-linked G6PD deficiency triggered by fava beans, infections, oxidative drugs).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Immune: IgG/IgM coating of RBCs causes splenic macrophages (extravascular) or complement-mediated membrane attack complex (intravascular) clearance. G6PD: NADPH lack causes Heinz body formation and intravascular/extravascular hemolysis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Anemia, jaundice, dark urine (hemoglobinuria), splenomegaly, back/flank pain during acute hemolytic crises.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Elevated reticulocyte count, elevated indirect bilirubin, high LDH, low haptoglobin; positive Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test in AIHA; G6PD enzyme assay (after acute crisis); Management: Corticosteroids/Rituximab for AIHA; avoid triggers in G6PD.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Malignant proliferation of immature hematopoietic progenitor cells (blasts) in bone marrow; ALL most common in children; AML most common in adults (linked to t(15;17) APML).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Clonal expansion of blast cells (> 20% in marrow) causes bone marrow failure (suppression of normal erythropoiesis, thrombopoiesis, and granulopoiesis) and tissue infiltration.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Abrupt onset of fever, severe fatigue, pallor, petechiae, purpura, bleeding, recurrent severe infections, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy (more in ALL), DIC in APML.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: CBC showing anemia, thrombocytopenia, variable WBC count; Peripheral film and marrow biopsy showing > 20% blasts; Auer rods in AML; TdT positive in ALL; Management: Induction chemotherapy (e.g. 7+3 for AML; ATRA for APML; multi-drug regimen for ALL).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Clonal myeloproliferative (CML) or lymphoproliferative (CLL) disorders. CML defined by t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL1 fusion); CLL defined by mature-appearing CD5+/CD19+ B-cells.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: CML: BCR-ABL1 constitutively active tyrosine kinase drives excessive granulocyte proliferation. CLL: Apoptosis failure leads to accumulation of incompetent mature CD5+ B lymphocytes.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: CML: Massive splenomegaly, weight loss, night sweats, gout, fatigue; risk of blast crisis. CLL: Asymptomatic lymphocytosis, generalized painless lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, B-symptoms, autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: CML: Marked leukocytosis with left shift (myelocytes, metamyelocytes), cytogenetics t(9;22); Management: Imatinib (TKI). CLL: Absolute lymphocytosis (> 5x10^9/L), 'smudge/smear cells' on blood film; Management: Fludarabine/Ibrutinib/Venetoclax.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Malignant neoplasms of lymphoid tissue; Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL) characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells; Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) includes B-cell (DLBCL, Follicular, Burkitt) and T-cell neoplasms.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Malignant transformation of lymphocytes within lymph nodes leading to nodular expansion, disruption of normal architecture, systemic B-symptoms, and extranodal dissemination.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Painless, rubbery lymphadenopathy (cervical, supraclavicular), alcohol-induced lymph node pain (in HL), B-symptoms (fever > 38C, drenching night sweats, weight loss > 10% in 6 months), hepatosplenomegaly.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Lymph node excisional biopsy: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+ 'owl-eye' nuclei) in HL; Immunophenotyping for NHL; Ann Arbor staging with PET/CT; Management: ABVD chemotherapy + radiotherapy for HL; R-CHOP for B-cell NHL.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Malignant proliferation of monoclonal plasma cells in bone marrow producing monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein), most commonly IgG or IgA.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Neoplastic plasma cells secrete osteoclast-activating factors (RANKL) causing lytic bone lesions, synthesize excess monoclonal immunoglobulin causing hyperviscosity and renal tubule damage (cast nephropathy).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: CRAB criteria: HyperCalcemia, Renal impairment, Anemia, Bone pain (especially back/ribs, pathological fractures), recurrent infections.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis (SPEP/UPEP) showing monoclonal M-spike; Bence Jones proteinuria; 'punched-out' lytic lesions on skeletal survey; marrow biopsy >= 10% plasma cells; Management: Bortezomib, Lenalidomide, Dexamethasone, autologous stem cell transplant.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: ITP: Autoimmune anti-GPIIb/IIIa destruction of platelets; DIC: Widespread systemic activation of coagulation cascade triggered by sepsis, trauma, malignancy, or obstetric emergencies.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: ITP: Opsonized platelets destroyed in spleen. DIC: Microvascular thrombosis causes organ failure, with secondary consumption of platelets and clotting factors leading to catastrophic bleeding.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: ITP: Mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, menorrhagia, NO splenomegaly. DIC: Oozing from venipuncture sites, mucosal bleeding, skin necrosis (purpura fulminans), shock.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: ITP: Isolated thrombocytopenia (< 100x10^9/L) with normal coagulation profile; Management: Corticosteroids (Prednisolone), IVIG, Splenectomy. DIC: Low platelets, prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer, schistocytes on blood film; Management: Treat underlying cause, FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) and B (Factor IX deficiency) are X-linked recessive bleeding disorders; von Willebrand Disease (vWD) is the most common autosomal dominant bleeding disorder.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Factor VIII/IX deficiency impairs intrinsic coagulation cascade; vWD impairs platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen and reduces Factor VIII half-life.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Hemophilia: Hemarthrosis (painful joint bleeding, destruction), deep muscle hematomas, post-surgical bleeding. vWD: Mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising, GI bleeding).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Hemophilia: Isolated prolonged APTT, normal PT and bleeding time, reduced Factor VIII/IX activity levels; Management: Recombinant Factor VIII/IX, Desmopressin (DDAVP). vWD: Prolonged APTT and bleeding time, reduced vWF antigen and Ristocetin cofactor activity; Management: Desmopressin (DDAVP), vWF-containing factor concentrates.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Systemic infection caused by Salmonella enterica serovars Typhi or Paratyphoid A, B, C; transmitted via fecal-oral route through contaminated food/water.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Bacteria invade intestinal M cells of Peyer's patches, disseminate through mesenteric lymph nodes into thoracic duct, causing secondary bacteremia and reticuloendothelial seeding.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), rose spots on abdomen, hepatosplenomegaly, pea-soup diarrhea or constipation; Red flags: intestinal perforation, GI hemorrhage.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Blood culture (gold standard 1st week); stool/urine culture (2nd-3rd week); Widal test (O & H titers); Primary Rx: IV Ceftriaxone or oral Azithromycin (due to fluoroquinolone resistance).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute secretory diarrheal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae (serogroups O1 and O139); transmitted by fecal-oral contamination of water supplies.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Cholera toxin (AB toxin) binds GM1 ganglioside, irreversibly activates adenylate cyclase, elevating intracellular cAMP and causing massive hypersecretion of water and electrolytes into gut lumen.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Profuse painless 'rice-water' liquid stools, fishy odor, projectile vomiting, severe dehydration (sunken eyes, washerwoman hands, loss of skin turgor), hypovolemic shock.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Darkfield microscopy (darting motility); stool culture on TCBS agar; Primary Rx: Aggressive oral rehydration therapy (ORS) or IV Ringer's Lactate; adjunctive Azithromycin or Doxycycline.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica following ingestion of mature quadrinucleate cysts in contaminated food/water.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Trophozoites invade colonic mucosa, creating classic 'flask-shaped' ulcers; hematogenous spread via portal circulation to liver causes liquefactive necrosis (amoebic liver abscess).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Dysentery with blood and mucus, abdominal colic, tenesmus; Liver abscess: RUQ pain, high fever, right shoulder pain, hepatomegaly; 'Anchovy sauce' brown pus on aspiration.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Stool microscopy (E. histolytica cysts/trophozoites with ingested RBCs); stool antigen/PCR; USG/CT abdomen for liver mass; Rx: Oral Metronidazole/Tinidazole followed by luminal agent (Paromomycin/Diloxanide furoate).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute intestinal infection caused by Shigella species (S. dysenteriae, S. flexneri, S. sonnei); highly contagious via fecal-oral route with low infectious dose (10-100 organisms).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Invades colonic epithelial cells, inducing intracellular replication and cell-to-cell spread; S. dysenteriae type 1 produces Shiga toxin, causing mucosal microvascular damage and HUS.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: High fever, severe abdominal cramps, tenesmus, frequent small-volume stools with frank blood, pus, and mucus; Red flags: Toxic megacolon, Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Stool microscopy (abundant PMNs and RBCs); stool culture on MacConkey/XLD agar; Primary Rx: Rehydration + Ciprofloxacin, Azithromycin, or Ceftriaxone.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Mosquito-borne protozoal infection transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes; caused by Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, or P. malariae.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Sporozoites infect hepatocytes (forming hypnozoites in vivax/ovale); merozoites invade RBCs causing synchronous hemolysis; P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) causes cytoadherence and microvascular sequestration.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Paroxysmal fever with chills/rigors, diaphoresis, splenomegaly, anemia, jaundice; Severe/Cerebral Malaria (P. falciparum): impaired consciousness, seizures, ARDS, severe anemia, hemoglobinuria (blackwater fever).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Giemsa-stained thick (sensitivity) and thin (species identification) blood films; Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs for PfHRP-2); Rx: Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT e.g. Artemether-Lumefantrine); IV Artesunate for severe malaria; Primaquine for relapse prevention (vivax/ovale after G6PD check).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Arboviral infection caused by Dengue Virus (serotypes DENV 1-4) transmitted by Aedes aegypti / Aedes albopictus mosquitoes.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Secondary infection with different serotype causes antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), triggering massive inflammatory cytokine release, endothelial dysfunction, and severe capillary permeability.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Sudden high fever ('breakbone fever'), severe retro-orbital headache, myalgias, arthralgias, maculopapular rash, positive tourniquet test; Severe Dengue: plasma leakage, pleural effusion/ascites, severe bleeding, dengue shock syndrome (DSS).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: NS1 antigen ELISA (days 1-5); IgM/IgG serology (after day 5); CBC (leukopenia, progressive thrombocytopenia, rising hematocrit indicating plasma leakage); Rx: Isotonic fluid management; Avoid NSAIDs/Aspirin due to bleeding risk.

Final Part 2 - Infectious Diseases Datab.Name: Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) & Neutropenic Fever

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: PUO: Fever > 38.3 C on multiple occasions for > 3 weeks without diagnosis. Neutropenic Fever: Fever >= 38.3 C with ANC < 500 cells/uL in oncology patients.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: In neutropenia, absence of mature neutrophils prevents normal localized inflammatory response, allowing minor mucosal translocation of pathogens to rapidly progress to fulminant bacteremia.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Persistent unexplained fever, rigors, mucositis, subtle catheter site erythema; Red flags: septic shock, rapid hemodynamic instability.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Blood cultures x 2 sets (peripheral and central lines), CBC with differential, CRP, CXR, urinalysis; Neutropenic Fever Rx: Immediate empiric broad-spectrum anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (Piperacillin-Tazobactam or Cefepime IV) within 1 hour.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV-1/2) infection transmitted via sexual contact, blood exposure, or vertical transmission.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Viral gp120 binds CD4 molecule and CCR5/CXCR4 co-receptors, infecting and destroying CD4+ T helper lymphocytes, causing progressive cellular immune deficiency.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Acute HIV syndrome (fever, LAD, rash); Asymptomatic phase; AIDS (CD4 < 200/uL): opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis pneumonia / PCP, Cryptococcal meningitis, CNS Toxoplasmosis, esophageal candidiasis, Kaposi sarcoma).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: 4th generation HIV 1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay; confirmatory HIV-1 RNA PCR; CD4 count & viral load monitoring; Primary Rx: Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART: 2 NRTIs + 1 NNRTI/INSTI e.g. Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir); Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 < 200.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Chronic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae; affects skin, peripheral nerves, and upper respiratory tract mucosa.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Cell-mediated immune response dictates spectrum: Tuberculoid (strong Th1 immunity, localized hypopigmented anesthetic plaques) vs Lepromatous (weak immunity, diffuse nodular skin lesions, high bacterial burden).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Hypopigmented or erythematous skin lesions with loss of sensation, thickened peripheral nerves (ulnar, common peroneal), claw hand, foot drop, leonine facies, painless trophic ulcers.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Slit-skin smear for Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB / Fite-Faraco stain); skin biopsy; Primary Rx: WHO Multidrug Therapy (MDT) — Paucibacillary (Rifampicin + Dapsone for 6 months), Multibacillary (Rifampicin + Dapsone + Clofazimine for 12 months).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Rabies: Lyssavirus transmitted via saliva from infected animal bite (dogs, bats). Tetanus: Clostridium tetani exotoxin (tetanospasmin) from soil-contaminated wounds.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Rabies virus travels retrograde via peripheral nerves to CNS causing encephalitis; Tetanospasmin retrogradely migrates to spinal cord, inhibiting Renshaw cell GABA/glycine release causing trismus and spasms.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Rabies: Hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation, hypersalivation, fatal encephalopathy; Tetanus: Trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, painful muscle spasms, opisthotonos.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): Thorough wound washing with soap & water for 15 min + Rabies Vaccine (days 0, 3, 7, 14) + Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) infiltrated into wound; Tetanus: Wound debridement + Tetanus Toxoid booster + Tetanus Immunoglobulin (TIG) for dirty wounds.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Post-infectious glomerulonephritis occurring 1-3 weeks after Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis or impetigo; common in children.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Immune complex deposition in glomerular subepithelial space (lumpy-bumpy appearance) activates complement cascade, recruiting neutrophils and causing glomerular inflammation.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Classic triad: Hematuria (smoky/cola-colored urine), Periorbital facial edema, and Hypertension. Oliguria, mild proteinuria, low-grade fever.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Ddx: ASO titer (high), Low C3 complement, Dysmorphic RBCs and Red Cell Casts on urinalysis. Treatment: Supportive, salt/fluid restriction, loop diuretics, antihypertensives.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Characterized by heavy proteinuria (> 3.5 g/24hr). Minimal Change (children), Membranous Nephropathy (adults, anti-PLA2R+), FSGS (adults/HIV/heroin).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Podocyte effacement or basement membrane damage leads to severe glomerular permeability loss to plasma proteins, particularly albumin.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Triad: Heavy proteinuria, Severe Hypoalbuminemia (< 30 g/L), Generalized Edema (anasarca). Hyperlipidemia, hypercoagulability (renal vein thrombosis), infection risk.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Urinalysis: 3-4+ protein, oval fat bodies; Serum albumin < 30 g/L; Lipid profile: hypercholesterolemia. Rx: Corticosteroids (1st line in MCD), ACEi/ARBs, diuretics, statins.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Abrupt decline in renal function over hours/days. Etiologies categorized into Prerenal (hypovolemia, sepsis), Intrinsic (ATN, AIN, AGN), and Postrenal (obstruction).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Prerenal: Renal hypoperfusion without structural damage. Intrinsic ATN: Ischemic or nephrotoxic tubular cell necrosis. Postrenal: Increased retrograde pressure.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6 hrs) or anuria, fluid overload (pulmonary edema, JVP elevation), uremic encephalopathy, pericarditis, hyperkalemic arrhythmias.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: KDIGO criteria: SCr increase >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48h or 1.5x baseline. FeNa < 1% (Prerenal) vs > 2% (ATN). Rx: Fluid resuscitation (prerenal), treat cause, Dialysis (AEIOU).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Progressive, irreversible loss of renal function (> 3 months). Leading causes: Diabetic Nephropathy, Hypertension, Chronic Glomerulonephritis.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Nephron loss leads to adaptive hyperfiltration in remaining nephrons, driving progressive glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and loss of excretory/endocrine functions.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Uremic frost, pruritus, fatigue, metallic taste, nausea, fluid retention, severe hypertension, renal anemia, metabolic bone disease (renal osteodystrophy), pericarditis.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2 or persistent albuminuria (> 30 mg/g). Bilaterally small shrunken kidneys on USG (except DM/polycystic). Rx: ACEi/ARBs, EPO, Phosphate binders, RRT.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Bacterial invasion of urinary tract. Most common pathogen: Escherichia coli (> 80%). Lower UTI (Cystitis) vs Upper UTI (Pyelonephritis).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Ascending infection from perineal flora up urethra to bladder (cystitis) and kidney parenchyma (pyelonephritis), triggering acute tubulointerstitial inflammation.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Cystitis: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain. Pyelonephritis: High fever, rigors, flank pain, CVA tenderness, nausea/vomiting, sepsis/bacteremia.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Urine Dipstick: Positive Nitrites and Leukocyte Esterase; Urine Microscopy: Pyuria (WBC > 10/hpf), WBC casts (pyelonephritis). Urine culture. Rx: Nitrofurantoin/TMP-SMX (cystitis), Ceftriaxone (pyelonephritis).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Serum Potassium > 5.5 mmol/L. Common in AKI, advanced CKD, K+-sparing diuretics, ACEi/ARBs, and tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Impaired renal potassium excretion or transcellular shift disrupts cardiac resting membrane potential, leading to lethal ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Often asymptomatic until severe; muscle weakness, flaccid paralysis, paresthesias, palpitations, bradycardia, cardiac arrest.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Serum K+ > 5.5 mmol/L. ECG changes: Tall tented T waves, prolonged PR, QRS widening, sine wave. Emergency Rx: IV Calcium Gluconate (membrane stabilization), IV Insulin + Dextrose, Salbutamol, Dialysis.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Common in young adult males.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Galactose-deficient IgA1 immune complexes deposit in glomerular mesangium, inducing mesangial proliferation and inflammatory cytokine cascade.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Recurrent episodes of gross (visible) hematuria occurring concurrently or within 1-2 days of an Upper Respiratory Tract Infection (synpharyngitic hematuria).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Renal biopsy: Mesangial IgA immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence. Normal complement levels. Rx: ACEi/ARBs for proteinuria, steroids in high risk.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Develops in ~30-40% of patients with long-standing Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Hyperglycemia drives efferent arteriolar constriction via RAAS, inducing glomerular hyperfiltration, nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions), and basement membrane thickening.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Persistent microalbuminuria progressing to overt proteinuria, worsening hypertension, progressive loss of eGFR, peripheral edema.
