details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR) 30-300 mg/g (micro) or > 300 mg/g (macro). Bilaterally enlarged/normal size kidneys on renal USG. Rx: Tight glycemic control, ACEi/ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Most common hereditary kidney disease; caused by mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16) or PKD2 (chromosome 4).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Defective polycystin protein impairs tubular epithelial differentiation, causing fluid-filled renal cysts that progressively destroy renal parenchyma.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Flank/abdominal pain, gross hematuria (cyst rupture), palpable bilateral flank masses, refractory hypertension, recurrent UTIs, intracranial berry aneurysms.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Renal Ultrasound: Multiple fluid-filled renal cysts bilaterally. Family history. Rx: BP control (ACEi/ARBs), Tolvaptan (vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist), Dialysis/Transplant for ESRD.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Accumulation of fluid in interstitial space. Major etiologies: Nephrotic Syndrome, Heart Failure, Cirrhosis, Malnutrition/Kwashiorkor.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Renal mechanism: Primary Na+ retention or hypoalbuminemia reducing plasma oncotic pressure (Starling forces), promoting fluid extravasation into interstitial tissue.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Bilateral pitting lower limb edema, sacral edema, ascites, pleural effusion, periorbital puffiness (pronounced in morning in renal cause).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Serum albumin, 24hr urine protein, U&Es, LFTs, Echocardiogram, Urine dipstick. Rx: Loop diuretics (Furosemide), dietary sodium restriction, treat underlying cause.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute focal neurological deficit caused by focal cerebral ischemia; thromboembolic or atherothrombotic occlusion of cerebral arteries (e.g. MCA, ACA).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Interruption of cerebral blood flow leads to ischemic cascade, ATP depletion, cytotoxic edema, and tissue infarction surrounding an ischemic penumbra.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Sudden contralateral hemiparesis/hemisensory loss (MCA: face/arm > leg; ACA: leg > arm), aphasia, dysarthria, hemianopia, gaze preference.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: NCCT Head (exclude hemorrhage, early ischemic signs); CT Angiography; tPA (Alteplase) within 4.5 hrs if no contraindications; Endovascular Thrombectomy within 6-24 hrs; Aspirin + Statin secondary prevention.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) due to chronic hypertension/amyloid angiopathy; Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) due to ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Rupture of vessel leads to hematoma formation, direct mass effect, elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), surrounding vasogenic edema, and secondary vasospasm.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: ICH: Sudden severe headache, vomiting, rapid neurological decline, elevated BP, coma. SAH: Sudden 'thunderclap' headache ('worst headache of life'), meningismus, loss of consciousness.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: NCCT Head (hyperdense blood in parenchyma or subarachnoid space); LP if CT negative for SAH (xanthochromia); Acute BP control (SBP < 140 mmHg for ICH); reversal of anticoagulation; Nimodipine for SAH vasospasm.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Medical emergency defined as continuous seizure activity lasting > 5 mins or >= 2 discrete seizures without full recovery of consciousness in between.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Failure of endogenous seizure termination mechanisms and persistent excessive hypersynchronous neuronal excitation causing cerebral hypoxia, lactic acidosis, and neuronal injury.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Continuous generalized tonic-clonic motor activity or subtle non-convulsive status; hyperthermia, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Bedside Fingerstick Glucose (exclude hypoglycemia); Stage 1 (0-10 min): IV Lorazepam 4mg or IM Midazolam 10mg; Stage 2 (10-30 min): IV Levetiracetam, Phenytoin/Fosphenytoin, or Valproate; Stage 3 (>30 min): ICU intubation + IV Propofol/Midazolam infusion.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Life-threatening infection of the leptomeninges; primary pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Listeria monocytogenes (elderly/immunocompromised).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Bacteria colonize nasopharynx, invade bloodstream, cross blood-brain barrier, and replicate in subarachnoid space, inducing intense purulent inflammatory response.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Classic triad: Fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status; Kernig and Brudzinski signs; purpuric/petechial rash (N. meningitidis); signs of raised ICP.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Lumbar Puncture CSF: High opening pressure, marked PMN leukocytosis (> 1000/uL), low glucose (< 40% serum ratio), high protein (> 100 mg/dL); Empiric IV Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin + Ampicillin (if >50 yrs) + Dexamethasone.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Aseptic meningitis commonly caused by Enteroviruses (Echovirus, Coxsackie); Encephalitis most commonly caused by Herpes Simplex Virus 1 (HSV-1).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Direct viral invasion and destruction of brain parenchyma (HSV-1 predilection for temporal lobes), triggering immune response, edema, and neuronal necrosis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Viral Meningitis: Fever, headache, photophobia, mild meningismus. HSV Encephalitis: Fever, severe headache, confusion, temporal lobe focal signs, dysphasia, seizures, behavioral changes.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: CSF: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein; HSV PCR in CSF; MRI Brain (temporal lobe hyperintensity); High-dose IV Acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8h) started immediately for suspected encephalitis.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy; often preceded 1-3 weeks by Campylobacter jejuni GI infection or respiratory viral infection.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Molecular mimicry between microbial lipooligosaccharides and peripheral nerve gangliosides leads to immune-mediated demyelination and axonal degeneration.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Symmetrical, progressive ascending muscle weakness starting in lower extremities, absent/hypoactive deep tendon reflexes, cranial nerve involvement (facial diplegia), autonomic instability.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: CSF: Albuminocytological dissociation (markedly elevated protein with normal WBC count); Nerve Conduction Studies (demyelinating patterns); IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) or Plasma Exchange; Steroids are INEFFECTIVE.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: State of unarousable unresponsiveness due to bilateral diffuse cortical dysfunction or focal lesion of the brainstem reticular activating system (RAS).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Etiologies categorized as Structural (stroke, hemorrhage, trauma, tumor) or Metabolic/Toxic (hypoxia, hypoglycemia, DKA, hepatic/uremic encephalopathy, drug overdose).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Unresponsiveness; abnormal respiratory patterns (Cheyne-Stokes); abnormal pupil responses (fixed dilated = herniation, pinpoint = opioid/pontine); motor posturing (decorticate/decerebrate).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS <= 8 = intubate); immediate 'Coma Cocktail' if indicated (Glucose, Thiamine, Naloxone); STAT NCCT Head; ABG, U&Es, LFTs, blood gas, toxic screen.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Transient, acute-onset global cognitive dysfunction characterized by fluctuating attention and awareness; common in hospitalized elderly patients.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Precipitated by underlying medical illness (UTI, pneumonia), electrolyte imbalances (hyponatremia), hypoxia, drug toxicity/withdrawal, or anticholinergic drugs.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention, disorganized thinking, altered level of consciousness, hallucinations, sleep-wake cycle reversal.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Clinical diagnosis using Confusion Assessment Method (CAM); workup includes CBC, U&Es, Urinalysis/Culture, CXR, ABG, medication review; primary treatment is identifying and treating underlying cause.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Includes Migraine (neurovascular), Cluster (trigeminal autonomic), Tension, and Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis (vasculitis in elderly).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Migraine: CGRP activation & trigeminovascular sensitization. GCA: Granulomatous inflammation of medium/large arteries leading to luminal occlusion and ischemic optic neuropathy.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Migraine: Unilateral throbbing, aura, nausea, photophobia. Cluster: Severe unilateral periorbital pain, lacrimation, rhinorrhea. GCA: New headache in >50yo, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual disturbance.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: GCA: Markedly elevated ESR (> 50-100 mm/hr) and CRP; urgent temporal artery biopsy; High-dose systemic steroids (Prednisolone 60mg or IV Methylprednisolone) immediately to prevent permanent blindness.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute or subacute compressive myelopathy resulting from vertebral metastases, epidural abscess, trauma, or herniated disc.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Extrinsic compression of the spinal cord impairs corticospinal, spinothalamic, and dorsal column pathways, causing ischemia and irreversible cord damage if untreated.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Bilateral lower limb weakness, sensory level on trunk, spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses (Babinski +), urinary retention/incontinence, localized back pain.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Urgent Whole Spine MRI; High-dose IV Dexamethasone (10-16 mg stat) for malignant cord compression to reduce vasogenic edema; urgent neurosurgical decompression or emergency radiotherapy.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Chronic inflammatory disorder of airways; hyper-responsiveness triggered by allergens, viral infections, exercise, or NSAIDs; reversible airflow limitation.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: IgE-mediated Type I hypersensitivity causing mast cell degranulation, bronchial smooth muscle constriction, airway mucosal edema, and mucous plugging.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Biphasic dyspnea, wheezing, cough, chest tightness. Red flags in acute severe asthma: inability to complete sentences in one breath, RR >= 25/min, pulse >= 110/min, PEFR 33-50% best/predicted. Silent chest = life-threatening.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Spirometry: FEV1/FVC < 0.70 with > 12% and 200mL bronchodilator reversibility. Peak Flow (PEFR) tracking. Emergency Tx: High-flow O2, inhaled SABA (Salbutamol) + SAMA (Ipratropium) nebulization, systemic corticosteroids (IV Hydrocortisone or oral Prednisolone), IV Magnesium sulfate if refractory.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Progressive, non-fully reversible airflow limitation caused by toxic gas/particle exposure (cigarette smoking > 90%). Comprises chronic bronchitis and emphysema.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Chronic inflammation destroys alveolar walls (loss of elastic recoil) and causes goblet cell hyperplasia with mucus hypersecretion. Exacerbations triggered by bacterial/viral infections.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Chronic cough, sputum production, progressive exertional dyspnea, barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing. Exacerbation red flags: increased dyspnea, sputum volume, and sputum purulence; cyanosis, drowsiness (hypercapnia).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Post-bronchodilator Spirometry: FEV1/FVC < 0.70 with minimal reversibility. ABG: Type 2 respiratory failure (hypoxemia + hypercapnia). Tx: Controlled O2 (Venturi mask 24-28% aiming SpO2 88-92%), nebulized bronchodilators, oral Prednisolone 30mg daily x 5 days, antibiotics (Amoxicillin/Doxycycline/Co-amoxiclav if purulent sputum), NIV if acidotic (pH < 7.35).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Acute infection of pulmonary parenchyma acquired outside healthcare settings. Most common pathogen: Streptococcus pneumoniae; atypical: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Pathogens breach lower respiratory mucosal defenses, replicating in alveoli and eliciting an acute inflammatory exudate that fills alveolar spaces (consolidation), impairing gas exchange.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Fever, rigors, productive cough with rusty/purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea. Physical findings: bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance, dullness to percussion, crackles.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: CXR: Lobar consolidation or patchy infiltrates. CURB-65 Score (Confusion, Urea > 7 mmol/L, RR >= 30, BP < 90/60, Age >= 65) guides admission/ICU. Tx: Low risk (CURB 0-1) oral Amoxicillin; Moderate/High risk (CURB 2+) IV Co-amoxiclav + oral Clarithromycin.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast bacillus). Transmitted via airborne droplets. Primary vs post-primary (reactivation) TB.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Inhaled bacilli engulfed by alveolar macrophages, forming caseating granulomas (Ghon focus/complex). Cell-mediated immunity (CD4+ T cells and INF-gamma) contains bacilli; reactivation occurs with immunosuppression.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Chronic cough > 2-3 weeks, hemoptysis, low-grade fever with evening rise, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia. Apical crackles on auscultation.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Sputum AFB stain (Ziegler-Neelsen) x 3, GeneXpert MTB/RIF (rapid DNA + Rifampicin resistance), CXR (upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, miliary mottling). Tx: 2 months RHZE (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) + 4 months RH. Pyridoxine (Vit B6) added to prevent Isoniazid neuropathy.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Pathological accumulation of fluid in pleural space. Transudative (systemic factors e.g., Heart Failure, Cirrhosis, Nephrotic) vs Exudative (local factors e.g., Pneumonia, TB, Malignancy).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Transudates arise from increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased oncotic pressure. Exudates arise from increased pleural capillary permeability or lymphatic obstruction.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, dry cough. Examination findings: Stony dull percussion note, decreased or absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance, tracheal deviation away from effusion (if large).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: CXR: Blunting of costophrenic angle (> 175mL), dense opacification with meniscus sign. Diagnostic Pleural Tap analyzed using Light's Criteria (Exudate if: Pleural/Serum Protein > 0.5, Pleural/Serum LDH > 0.6, or Pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit normal). Tx: Treat underlying cause; therapeutic thoracocentesis or chest drain.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Air in pleural space causing lung collapse. Primary spontaneous (rupture of subpleural blebs in tall, thin young men) vs Secondary (COPD/TB) vs Tension pneumothorax.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Tension pneumothorax: One-way valve mechanism allows air to enter pleural space during inspiration but prevents escape during expiration, increasing intrathoracic pressure, collapsing lung, and shifting mediastinum, compromising venous return.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Sudden onset severe pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Physical findings: Hyper-resonant percussion, absent breath sounds, reduced chest expansion. Tension features: Hypotension, severe cyanosis, tracheal deviation away from affected side, JVP elevation.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: CXR (spontaneous): Visceral pleural line visible with absence of lung markings peripherally. (Tension is a CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS - DO NOT DELAY Tx FOR CXR!). Tx Tension: Immediate needle decompression (14G cannula in 2nd ICS anterior mid-clavicular line or 5th ICS anterior axillary line), followed by Intercostal Chest Drain (ICD).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Coughing up of blood originating from respiratory tract below vocal cords. Major causes: Bronchiectasis, Tuberculosis, Bronchogenic Carcinoma, Pneumonia, Aspergilloma, Pulmonary Embolism.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Bleeding typically arises from hypervascular bronchial circulation (high pressure) damaged by chronic inflammation, erosion, necrotizing infection, or tumor invasion.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Expectoration of bright red frothy blood mixed with sputum. Massive hemoptysis (> 100-600 mL in 24 hrs) threatens airway occlusion and asphyxiation.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: CXR, Sputum AFB and cytology, CT Chest (high resolution), Bronchoscopy. Tx Massive: Maintain airway (position bleeding side down), high-flow O2, rigid/flexible bronchoscopy, Bronchial Artery Embolization (BAE), surgical resection if refractory.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Inability of respiratory system to maintain adequate gas exchange. Type 1 (Hypoxemic) vs Type 2 (Hypercapnic).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Type 1: V/Q mismatch or diffusion impairment causes hypoxemia (PaO2 < 60 mmHg / 8 kPa) with normal or low PaCO2 (< 45 mmHg / 6 kPa). Type 2: Alveolar hypoventilation causes hypoxemia with hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg / 6 kPa).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Type 1 features: Cyanosis, tachypnea, tachycardia, confusion. Type 2 features: Bounding pulse, flapping tremor (asterixis), warm peripheries, papilledema, drowsiness, acidotic breath.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) analysis. Type 1 causes: Pneumonia, Pulmonary Edema, PE, ARDS, Asthma. Type 2 causes: COPD, Severe Asthma, Narcotics overdose, Myasthenia Gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome. Tx: High-flow O2 for Type 1; Controlled O2 + NIV/mechanical ventilation for Type 2.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Systemic autoimmune disease with strong female predominance (9:1); peak onset 15-45 yrs; strongly associated with HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Type III (immune complex) and Type II hypersensitivity; loss of self-tolerance leads to antinuclear autoantibody production, immune complex deposition in tissues, complement activation, and organ damage.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Malar 'butterfly' rash (spares nasolabial folds), discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral/nasal painless ulcers, non-erosive arthritis, serositis (pleuritis, pericarditis), renal involvement (lupus nephritis), CNS lupus (seizures, psychosis).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: ANA (sensitive >95% screening test); Anti-dsDNA (highly specific, correlates with disease activity & nephritis); Anti-Smith (most specific); decreased C3/C4 complement levels; Hydroxychloroquine (mainstay for all), Steroids, Cyclophosphamide/Belimumab for nephritis.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Chronic systemic inflammatory autoimmune disease primarily targetting synovial joints; female-to-male ratio 3:1; linked to HLA-DR4.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Autoimmune synovitis with pannus formation (proliferative synovial membrane) that erodes articular cartilage and underlying bone; driven by TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Symmetrical polyarthritis affecting PIP, MCP, and MTP joints (spares DIP joints); morning stiffness >1 hour; joint deformities (ulnar deviation, Swan-neck, Boutonniere); extra-articular features (rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, Felty syndrome).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Anti-Citrullinated Protein Antibodies (Anti-CCP / ACPA, 98% specific); Rheumatoid Factor (RF); elevated ESR/CRP; X-ray showing juxta-articular osteopenia and joint space narrowing; Early DMARD therapy (Methotrexate + Folic acid mainstay, Leflunomide, Biologics like Anti-TNF Etanercept/Infliximab).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Prototypic seronegative spondyloarthropathy; strong association with HLA-B27 (>90%); predominantly affects young males (15-30 yrs).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Chronic inflammation at entheses (sites of tendon/ligament attachment to bone), particularly sacroiliac joints, followed by progressive ossification, syndesmophyte formation, and spinal fusion.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Inflammatory back pain (insidious onset <45 yrs, improves with exercise, worsens with rest, nocturnal awakenings), morning stiffness, reduced spinal mobility (Schober's test <5 cm expansion), acute anterior uveitis (painful red eye), apical lung fibrosis, aortic regurgitation.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Negative RF/Anti-CCP; positive HLA-B27; X-ray/MRI showing sacroiliitis, 'bamboo spine' (bridging syndesmophytes), dagger sign; First-line: NSAIDs (continuous), exercise/physiotherapy; Secukinumab (IL-17i) or Anti-TNF agents for refractory cases.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Metabolic disease characterized by hyperuricemia (serum urate > 6.8 mg/dL / >400 umol/L); more common in men; triggered by purine-rich diet, alcohol, loop diuretics, or renal impairment.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Supersaturation and deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid and soft tissues, triggering inflammasome activation, IL-1beta release, and severe neutrophilic joint inflammation.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Monoarthritis presenting as sudden onset of excruciating pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth at 1st metatarsophalangeal joint (Podagra); tophi formation (chalky urate deposits in ears, tendons, joints) in chronic gout; renal calculi.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Arthrocentesis: Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals under polarized light; Acute attack: Colchicine, NSAIDs (Indomethacin/Naproxen), or Intra-articular/Oral Steroids; Chronic urate-lowering therapy: Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) or Febuxostat (start AFTER acute attack subsides).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in hyaline and fibrocartilage; common in elderly; associated with hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia, and hypothyroidism.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Precipitation of CPPD crystals in articular cartilage leads to shedding into joint space, provoking inflammatory response resembling acute gout or osteoarthritis.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Acute monoarthritis or oligoarthritis, most commonly affecting large joints like the knee, wrist, or shoulder; joint effusion and tenderness; chronic CPPD arthropathy resembles OA.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Arthrocentesis: Rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals; X-ray shows chondrocalcinosis (linear calcification of articular cartilage/fibrocartilage menisci); Management: Intra-articular steroid injection, oral NSAIDs, or Colchicine.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Autoimmune disorder characterized by vascular dysfunction, autoimmunity, and widespread tissue fibrosis affecting skin and internal organs; marked female excess.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Endothelial injury causes microvascular obliteration; dysregulated fibroblast activation leads to excessive deposition of collagen and extracellular matrix in skin, lungs, GI tract, and kidneys.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Limited Cutaneous (CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia); Diffuse Cutaneous (rapid skin thickening proximal to elbows/knees, early interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis with malignant hypertension).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Anti-Centromere antibodies (highly specific for Limited SSc / CREST); Anti-Scl-70 / Anti-topoisomerase I (associated with Diffuse SSc & ILD); Anti-RNA Polymerase III (associated with Scleroderma Renal Crisis); Management: ACE inhibitors for renal crisis (life-saving!), Calcium channel blockers (Nifedipine) for Raynaud's, Cyclophosphamide/Mycophenolate for ILD.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Systemic autoimmune disorders causing chronic inflammation of skeletal muscle; Dermatomyositis includes cutaneous features and strong association with underlying malignancy.

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Polymyositis: CD8+ T-cell mediated endomysial inflammation damaging muscle fibers. Dermatomyositis: Complement-mediated microangiopathy causing perimysial inflammation and cutaneous lesions.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Symmetrical, progressive proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from chair, climbing stairs, combing hair); Dermatomyositis rash: Heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital edema), Gottron's papules (erythematous scaly papules over MCP/PIP joints), Shawl sign, Mechanic's hands; dysphagia; interstitial lung disease.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Markedly elevated Serum Creatine Kinase (CK) and Aldolase; Anti-Jo-1 (anti-synthetase syndrome: myositis + ILD + arthritis + mechanic's hands); Anti-Mi-2 (specific for DM); EMG showing myopathic triad; Muscle biopsy (gold standard); Management: High-dose oral Corticosteroids (Prednisolone) first-line, Methotrexate/Azathioprine as steroid-sparing agents.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Large-vessel systemic vasculitis predominantly affecting branches of external carotid artery in patients >50 years; strongly associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Granulomatous inflammation of vessel wall with multinucleated giant cells causing lumen stenosis, ischemia, and risk of irreversible anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (blindness).

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication (pain when chewing), visual disturbances (amaurosis fugax, sudden painless vision loss), systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss). PMR: aching/stiffness in neck, shoulder, and pelvic girdles.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Markedly elevated ESR (>50-100 mm/hr) and CRP; Temporal artery biopsy showing granulomatous vasculitis with giant cells and disruption of internal elastic lamina; Management: Immediate high-dose oral Steroids (Prednisolone 40-60 mg daily; IV Methylprednisolone if visual loss) BEFORE awaiting biopsy results to prevent permanent blindness.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: ANCA-associated small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis classically involving upper respiratory tract, lower respiratory tract, and kidneys (triad).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA / anti-PR3) activate neutrophils, leading to endothelial damage, necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, and small vessel destruction.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Upper airway: chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting, saddle-nose deformity, otitis media; Lower airway: hemoptysis, cough, dyspnea, cavitating pulmonary nodules; Renal: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (crescents), hematuria, proteinuria.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: c-ANCA positive (Anti-Proteinase 3 / Anti-PR3 antibodies in >90%); Urinalysis showing dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts; Tissue biopsy showing necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis; Management: Remission induction with Cyclophosphamide or Rituximab + High-dose Corticosteroids.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Etiology
details.content: Chronic systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands (salivary and lacrimal); 9:1 female excess; primary or secondary (associated with RA, SLE).

details.title: Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology
details.content: Lymphocytic infiltration (CD4+ T cells, B cells) and destruction of lacrimal and salivary exocrine epithelial cells leading to exocrine glandular dysfunction and dryness.

details.title: Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags
details.content: Sicca complex: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes, gritty sensation), Xerostomia (dry mouth, dental caries, difficulty swallowing dry food), parotid gland enlargement, extraglandular features (arthralgias, Raynaud's, interstitial lung disease, increased risk of Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management
details.content: Positive Anti-SSA / Anti-Ro and Anti-SSB / Anti-La antibodies; positive ANA and RF; Schirmer's test (<5 mm wetting in 5 mins); Ocular Rose Bengal staining; Minor salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis; Management: Artificial tears, artificial saliva, Pilocarpine (muscarinic agonist), Hydroxychloroquine for systemic symptoms.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Secretory type (sIgA) is a dimer/trimer with a J-chain and a secretory piece; monomer in serum. Produced by mucosal plasma cells.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Provides mucosal immunity; dimer secretory piece resists digestive enzymes and coats/neutralizes pathogens on mucosal surfaces, preventing epithelial attachment.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Selective IgA Deficiency (causes recurrent sinopulmonary and GI infections); IgA Nephropathy (Berger's disease); Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Serum IgA levels (<7 mg/dL defines selective deficiency); immunofluorescence showing IgA mesangial deposits in kidney biopsy.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Most abundant class in serum (~75%); monomeric structure. Secreted in high amounts by plasma cells during the secondary adaptive immune response.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Functions as a primary defender against bacteria, viruses, and toxins via neutralization, opsonization (promoting macrophage phagocytosis via Fc receptor binding), complement activation, and ADCC via NK cells; uniquely crosses the placenta.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Erythroblastosis Fetalis (Type II hypersensitivity); IgG autoantibody deficiencies cause recurrent pyogenic infections.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Quantitative serum IgG levels; immunofluorescence showing IgG deposition; positive Coombs test (for autoimmune hemolytic anemia).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Pentameric structure linked by disulfide bonds and a J-chain in secretions; monomeric on mature B cell surfaces as a B cell receptor (BCR). Earliest antibody produced in a primary immune response.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Exhibits high avidity with 10 antigen-binding sites; exceptionally potent at complement activation (complement fixing) and causing agglutination (clumping) of pathogens.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Mismatched ABO blood transfusion reactions (Type II hypersensitivity); participates in Type III immune complex-mediated hypersensitivities; cold agglutinin disease.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Quantitative serum IgM levels; isohemagglutinin titer; direct/indirect agglutination assays.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Monomeric structure; co-expressed with IgM on the surface of mature, naive B lymphocytes. Very low concentration in normal serum (~0.2%).

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Functions primarily as a membrane-bound antigen receptor (BCR partner) to assist in B cell activation, maturation, and survival signaling.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Hyper-IgD syndrome (a periodic fever syndrome marked by high IgD levels and recurrent inflammatory episodes); levels vary in chronic inflammatory diseases.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry showing surface IgD+ on mature naive B cells (CD19+ / CD20+ / IgM+ / IgD+); serum IgD levels measured by ELISA or nephelometry.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Lowest concentration in normal serum; monomeric structure with an extra constant domain (CH4). Produced by plasma cells following isotype switching induced by IL-4.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds with extremely high affinity to FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils. Cross-linking by allergens triggers immediate cell degranulation, releasing preformed inflammatory mediators.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Mediates Type I hypersensitivity (allergic rhinitis, asthma, hives, systemic anaphylaxis); plays an essential defensive role against helminthic parasite infections.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Elevated total serum IgE levels; allergen-specific IgE testing (RAST/ImmunoCAP); skin prick wheel-and-flare testing.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Highly pure, monospecific antibodies manufactured in vitro. Produced by fusing a specific plasma B cell with an immortal myeloma cell to create a hybridoma.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds with absolute specificity to a single epitope on a target antigen, enabling targeted neutralisation, cell labeling, or receptor blocking.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Used as therapeutics: Rituximab (anti-CD20 for B cell lymphoma and RA), Infliximab (anti-TNF-α for Crohn's and RA), Trastuzumab (anti-HER2 for breast cancer).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Purity checked via capillary electrophoresis; binding specificity validated via ELISA and Western blot.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Rapid, IgE-mediated systemic or local allergic reaction occurring within minutes of re-exposure to an allergen in a sensitized individual.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Allergen cross-links IgE antibodies pre-bound to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells/basophils. Degranulation releases histamine (early phase) and stimulates leukotriene synthesis (late phase).

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Anaphylactic shock (marked by massive systemic vasodilation, bronchial smooth muscle contraction, and laryngeal edema); allergic asthma; food allergies.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Clinical diagnosis; elevated serum tryptase (marker of mast cell degranulation) measured shortly after the episode; skin prick testing.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction targeting antigens present on specific cell surfaces or within extracellular matrix tissues.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: IgG or IgM antibodies bind directly to target cells, triggering classical complement activation (MAC lysis), opsonization for phagocytosis, or NK cell-mediated ADCC.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Mismatched ABO blood transfusion reactions, Erythroblastosis Fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn), Myasthenia Gravis, Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia, Goodpasture's syndrome.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Direct and Indirect Coombs tests; detection of tissue-specific autoantibodies (e.g., anti-AChR); immunofluorescence biopsy showing linear deposition.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Immune complex-mediated inflammatory reaction caused by the deposition of circulating, medium-sized antigen-antibody complexes in filters and tissues.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Circulating complexes deposit in blood vessels, joint synovium, or glomeruli, where they activate complement and recruit neutrophils that release destructive lysosomal enzymes.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), Serum Sickness, Arthus reaction, Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Decreased serum C3 and C4 complement levels; presence of circulating immune complexes; tissue biopsies showing granular (lumpy) immune deposits under immunofluorescence.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Delayed-type, cell-mediated (antibody-independent) inflammatory reaction; peaks 48-72 hours after physical skin contact with an active hapten.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Haptens (e.g., poison ivy pentadecacatechol, nickel, leather chemicals) bind self-proteins, becoming immunogenic. Dendritic cells present them to Th1 cells, which secrete IFN-γ to recruit and activate highly destructive macrophages.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Pruritic, vesicular, erythematous skin lesions localized to the area of contact; localized tissue injury and swelling; Tuberculin skin test; graft rejection.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Patch testing (application of suspected allergens to the skin for 48 hours to observe for a localized cell-mediated reaction); Tuberculin skin test (PPD measurement).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Systemic autoimmune disease showing a strong female predominance (9:1); strongly associated with HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3 alleles.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Mediates a Type III hypersensitivity reaction; autoantibodies bind to self-antigens (DNA/histones), forming immune complexes that deposit in small vessels and filters, activating complement and recruiting destructive neutrophils.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Malar 'butterfly' rash, discoid lupus, lupus nephritis (glomerulonephritis), arthritis, hematologic cytopenias, and neurological symptoms.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Positive ANA (sensitive screening); Anti-dsDNA and Anti-Smith autoantibodies (highly specific); decreased serum C3 and C4 complement levels.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Systemic inflammatory disease affecting joints; strong association with HLA-DR4. Characterized by the presence of Rheumatoid Factor (RF).

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Mediates a mixed Type III/IV hypersensitivity. Autoreactive Th1 cells recruit macrophages that release destructive TNF-α in joint synovium. RF (IgM binding to IgG Fc tails) forms immune complexes that amplify inflammation.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Symmetrical polyarthritis (morning stiffness, joint erosions, pannus formation), subcutaneous nodules, systemic vasculitis, and pulmonary fibrosis.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Positive Rheumatoid Factor (RF); highly specific Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies; elevated ESR and CRP.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity; highly associated with HLA-DR3; often associated with thymic hyperplasia or thymoma.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Autoantibodies (IgG) bind to and block nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction, triggering receptor internalization, complement-mediated destruction, and impaired synaptic transmission.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Progressive muscle weakness and fatiguability (worse with exercise, improves with rest), ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and potentially fatal respiratory failure (myasthenic crisis).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Anti-AChR antibodies (highly specific); Anti-Muscle-Specific Tyrosine Kinase (MuSK) antibodies; electromyography (EMG) decremental response.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Group of genetic disorders; most common is X-linked (IL2RG mutation). Autosomal recessive forms include adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency and RAG1/RAG2 mutations.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Severe defect in both cellular and humoral immunity. RAG1/RAG2 mutations block the V(D)J recombination needed to build functional B and T cell receptors, leaving lymphocytes totally non-functional.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Infants present with severe, recurrent infections (bacterial, viral, fungal, protozoal), chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and absence of thymic shadow. Fatal in infancy without bone marrow transplant.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Absent or extremely low T and B cell counts on flow cytometry; absence of T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) on newborn screening.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: X-linked recessive immunodeficiency caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the Bruton's Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) gene on chromosome Xq22.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: BTK is required for pre-B cell receptor signaling; its defect blocks pre-B cells from maturing into mature B cells in the bone marrow, causing a near-total absence of B cells and all immunoglobulin classes.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Male infants present after age 3-6 months (as maternal IgG wanes) with recurrent, severe pyogenic bacterial infections (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) of the respiratory tract.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Profound B-cell lymphopenia (<1% CD19+ B cells in peripheral blood) on flow cytometry; extremely low or undetectable levels of serum IgG, IgA, and IgM.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Congenital immunodeficiency caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 22q11.2, resulting in defective development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Causes thymic hypoplasia or aplasia, resulting in deficient T cell maturation and impaired cell-mediated immunity. Also causes parathyroid hypoplasia, leading to low calcium.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Recurrent viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections; cleft palate; congenital heart defects (conotruncal anomalies); tetany due to severe hypocalcemia.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Absent or profoundly low CD3+ T cell counts with normal B cell counts; absence of thymic shadow on chest X-ray; FISH/microarray showing 22q11.2 microdeletion.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Acquired clonal stem cell disorder caused by a somatic mutation in the PIGA gene, leading to a deficiency of GPI-anchor proteins.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Loss of GPI anchors causes a complete deficiency of cell-surface complement regulators DAF (CD55) and CD59 (MIRL), leaving red blood cells highly vulnerable to uncontrolled bystander complement-mediated MAC lysis.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Intravascular hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinuria (dark morning urine), severe thrombosis (especially in atypical venous sites), and pancytopenia.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry analysis showing absence of CD55 and CD59 on red blood cells and granulocytes.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Encoded by classical HLA-A, B, and C genes. Composed of an alpha heavy chain and a non-polymorphic beta-2 microglobulin chain. Distributed on all nucleated cells.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds and displays endogenous peptide antigens (viral or mutated intracellular proteins processed by proteasomes) to CD8+ Cytotoxic T cells.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Crucial for viral clearance and tumor surveillance; down-regulated by many viruses to escape detection; HLA-B27 strongly associated with Ankylosing Spondylitis.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry for surface MHC Class I/HLA expression; DNA-based molecular HLA typing.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Encoded by classical HLA-DP, DQ, and DR genes. Composed of an alpha and beta heterodimer. Expressed primarily on professional Antigen Presenting Cells (APCs).

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds and displays exogenous peptide antigens (extracellular pathogens processed via the endosomal-lysosomal pathway) to CD4+ Helper T cells.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Key mediator of CD4+ T helper cell activation and immune collaboration; HLA-DR4 associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis; HLA-DR3/DR4 associated with Type 1 Diabetes.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry for HLA-DP, DQ, DR; PCR-based HLA typing.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Originates in the bone marrow; resides as immature sentinel cells in peripheral tissues. The most potent 'professional' Antigen Presenting Cells (APCs).

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Captures, processes, and displays exogenous antigens on MHC Class II (and Class I via cross-presentation). Matures and migrates to lymph nodes to express co-stimulatory molecules (B7) and activate naive T cells.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Acts as the essential bridge between innate and adaptive immunity; crucial for initiating primary adaptive immune responses and maintaining central/peripheral self-tolerance.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry identification using surface markers CD11c, HLA-DR, CD80, CD83, and CD86.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Derived from circulating blood monocytes; differentiates into tissue-specific residents (e.g., microglia, Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages). Activated by IFN-γ or PAMPs.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Functions as professional phagocytes that engulf and digest pathogens/debris. Acts as APCs displaying antigens on MHC Class II to effector T cells at the site of inflammation; secretes pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α).

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Primary cells involved in chronic inflammation, granuloma formation (e.g., in tuberculosis and leprosy), and the pathogenesis of septic shock (via excessive TNF-α release).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Immunohistochemical staining or flow cytometry using markers CD14, CD68, CD11b, and HLA-DR.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Large granular lymphocytes originating from lymphoid progenitors but functioning as part of the innate immune system. No antigen-specific receptors.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Recognizes and destroys virus-infected and tumor cells. Employs the 'missing self' hypothesis to target cells lacking MHC Class I; also executes ADCC via Fc receptor CD16.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Involved in early defense against intracellular infections (especially herpesviruses) and cancers; defects lead to severe recurrent viral infections.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry markers CD3- and CD56+ / CD16+; functional NK cytotoxicity assays.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Differentiated CD4+ T helper cell subset. Development is promoted by IL-12 and IFN-γ; driven by the T-bet transcription factor.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Drives cell-mediated immunity against intracellular pathogens. Secretes IFN-γ to strongly activate macrophages, IL-2 to promote T cell proliferation, and TNF-β to mediate localized tissue inflammation.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Orchestrates Type IV Delayed-Type Hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., Tuberculin skin test, contact dermatitis); implicated in chronic inflammatory autoimmune diseases like Crohn's disease.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Intracellular cytokine staining for IFN-γ; CD4+ T cell flow cytometry panel; positive Tuberculin (PPD) skin test.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Differentiated CD4+ T helper cell subset. Differentiation is induced by IL-4; driven by the GATA3 transcription factor.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Promotes humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity and defense against extracellular parasites (helminths). Secretes IL-4 (induces IgE class switching), IL-5 (recruits/activates eosinophils), and IL-10 (suppresses Th1 responses).

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Implicated in Type I hypersensitivity allergic reactions (asthma, eczema, anaphylaxis); genetic predisposition to atopy.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Intracellular cytokine staining for IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13; elevated serum IgE levels; peripheral blood eosinophilia.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Differentiated CD4+ T helper cell subset. Differentiation is promoted by IL-6, TGF-β, and IL-23; driven by the RORγt transcription factor.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Recruits neutrophils and maintains mucosal/epithelial barriers against extracellular bacteria and fungi by secreting IL-17 and IL-22.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Autosomal dominant Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome) has Th17 deficiency; overactivity is associated with psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Intracellular cytokine staining for IL-17 via flow cytometry; serum IL-17 assay.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Subclass of CD4+ T cells characterized by the expression of CD25 and the Foxp3 transcription factor. Originates in thymus (nTregs) or peripheral tissues (iTregs).

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Enforces peripheral self-tolerance by active suppression of self-reactive lymphocytes. Secretes anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β; utilizes CTLA-4 to downregulate co-stimulatory molecules on APCs.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: IPEX syndrome (severe autoimmune disease marked by enteropathy, dermatological lesions, and polyendocrinopathy) is caused by Foxp3 mutation. Cancers recruit Tregs to escape immune destruction.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry showing CD4+ CD25+ Foxp3+; Foxp3 gene analysis.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Originates in the bone marrow and matures in the thymus (passing positive and negative selection). Recognizes peptide antigens presented on MHC Class I molecules.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Directly kills virus-infected, damaged, or tumor cells by inducing apoptosis. Employs the perforin/granzyme pathway (to form membrane pores and digest targets) and the Fas/FasL death receptor pathway.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Essential for viral clearance and tumor surveillance; implicated in transplant rejection (host-versus-graft disease) and Type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry identification using CD3+ and CD8+ surface markers; granzyme B and perforin enzyme-linked immunospot (ELISPOT) assays.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: The most abundant complement protein in serum, produced mainly by the liver. Acts as the central convergence point for all three complement activation pathways.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Cleaved into C3a (anaphylatoxin that recruits mast cells/neutrophils) and C3b (binds covalently to pathogens to mediate opsonization, and forms C5 convertases to amplify the terminal pathway).

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Congenital C3 deficiency leads to severe, recurrent pyogenic infections (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) and severe immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Serum C3 quantitative levels (using nephelometry or radial immunodiffusion); CH50 and AH50 hemolytic complement assays.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Liver-synthesized serum glycoprotein. Cleaved by C5 convertases (C4b2a3b in classical/lectin; C3b2Bb in alternative) to initiate the terminal complement cascade.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Cleaved into C5a (a highly potent anaphylatoxin and neutrophil chemoattractant) and C5b. C5b sequentially binds C6, C7, C8, and multiple C9 proteins to form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC/C5b-9).

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: C5 deficiency or terminal MAC pathway defects (C5-C9) result in high susceptibility to recurrent, life-threatening Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Serum C5 quantitative levels; CH50 assay (decreased/absent with normal C3 and C4 indicates terminal pathway deficiency).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Produced primarily by activated CD4+ T helper (Th1) cells; acts as a crucial autocrine and paracrine T cell growth factor.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds to high-affinity IL-2 receptors (containing CD25) to trigger clonal expansion, proliferation, and survival of T cells, B cells, NK cells, and regulatory T cells (Tregs).

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Recombinant IL-2 (Aldesleukin) is used to treat metastatic renal cell carcinoma and melanoma; targeted by immunosuppressive drugs like Cyclosporine and Tacrolimus.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Serum cytokine assays; expression of CD25 (alpha chain of IL-2R) on the surface of T lymphocytes by flow cytometry.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Secreted by CD4+ Th2 cells, mast cells, and activated basophils. Classic pleiotropic cytokine.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Induces differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into the Th2 helper phenotype. Directs B cell class-switching to IgE and IgG4, and promotes eosinophil tissue recruitment.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Key driver of atopic allergic reactions (allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis); targeted by Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Serum IL-4 level by ELISA; intracellular cytokine staining on T cells.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Type II interferon; homodimeric glycoprotein produced mainly by activated CD4+ Th1 cells, CD8+ CTLs, and Natural Killer (NK) cells.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds to Type II IFN receptors to activate the JAK-STAT pathway. Acts as the primary battle cytokine that activates macrophages, enhances MHC Class I and II expression on APCs, and blocks IL-4-induced IgE switching.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Recombinant IFN-γ (Actimmune) is used to treat Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) by boosting macrophage bactericidal activity; crucial for tuberculosis clearance.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: IFN-γ release assays (IGRA) for tuberculosis screening (e.g., QuantiFERON-TB Gold); intracellular cytokine flow cytometry.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Homotrimeric cytokine produced mainly by activated macrophages, T cells, and NK cells in response to PAMP/DAMP recognition.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Coordinates local and systemic inflammation. Induces vascular endothelium adhesion molecules, increases vascular permeability, recruits neutrophils, and triggers hepatocytes to release acute-phase proteins.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Central mediator of rheumatoid arthritis joint destruction, Crohn's disease inflammation, and septic shock; triggers cachexia (wasting syndrome) in chronic infections and malignancy.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Serum TNF-α concentration; acute-phase reactants (CRP and ESR) as surrogates.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Family of calcium-dependent carbohydrate-binding transmembrane proteins. L-selectin on leukocytes; E- and P-selectin on activated endothelial cells.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Interacts with mucin-like ligands (CD15s) to mediate the initial weak, transient 'rolling' phase of leukocyte extravasation along vessel walls.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Deficient selectin ligand expression causes Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 2 (LAD II), presenting with severe immune deficiencies, high leukocytosis, and developmental delay.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry evaluating CD15s (sialyl Lewis X) expression on neutrophils; genetic testing for SLC35C1 mutations.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Heterodimeric cell-surface glycoproteins composed of non-covalently associated alpha and beta subunits. Examples include LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18) and Mac-1.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds tightly to immunoglobulin-superfamily ligands (like ICAM-1) on endothelial cells, converting leukocyte 'rolling' into stable 'tight adhesion' during extravasation.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Loss-of-function mutation in the common beta-2 integrin chain CD18 gene causes Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1 (LAD I), marked by recurrent infections without pus, delayed umbilical cord separation.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Flow cytometry confirming complete or partial absence of surface CD18/CD11b on peripheral blood granulocytes.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Small, non-proteinaceous chemical compound of low molecular weight (e.g., penicillin, urushiol in poison ivy). It is reactive but non-immunogenic on its own.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds covalently to a high-molecular-weight host carrier protein, creating a hapten-carrier complex that is recognized as foreign, stimulating antibody and T-cell responses.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Drug-induced autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Type II hypersensitivity); urushiol contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity).

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Clinical diagnosis; allergen patch testing; specific IgE or drug-induced antibody screening.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Bacterial or viral proteins (e.g., S. aureus TSST-1, S. pyogenes exotoxins) that bypass normal MHC presentation rules.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Binds directly and simultaneously to the outer face of MHC Class II molecules on APCs and the Vβ domain of T-cell receptors (TCRs), cross-linking them without processing. Activates up to 20% of all T cells.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Triggers Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) and food poisoning, inducing a catastrophic 'cytokine storm' (massive release of TNF-α, IL-1, IFN-γ) leading to severe fever, hypotension, and shock.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Bacterial cultures from infection sites; TSST-1 toxin detection via PCR or immunological assays; multi-organ failure screening (CMP, lactate).

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay. A highly sensitive, solid-phase in vitro serological diagnostic method using microtiter plates.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Combines antibody-antigen binding specificity with enzyme-catalyzed substrate reactions (e.g., using horseradish peroxidase) to produce a quantifiable color change.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Standard screening method for HIV antibodies, food allergies (specific IgE), autoimmune disease autoantibodies (e.g., anti-dsDNA), and circulating cytokines.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Spectrophotometric reading of optical density (OD) to quantify target concentrations.

details.title: Key Characteristics & Origin
details.content: Vaccines made from weakened (attenuated) live pathogens that maintain their replication capacity but lose their pathogenicity.

details.title: Primary Function & Mechanism
details.content: Replicates transiently inside host cells, delivering vaccine antigens to both MHC Class I and Class II pathways, generating highly durable humoral and cellular (memory CD8+ CTL) immunity.

details.title: Clinical & Disease Associations
details.content: Examples: Measles, Mumps, Rubella (MMR), Varicella, Oral Polio (Sabin). Contraindicated in pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals due to safety/reversion risks.

details.title: Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests
details.content: Serological antibody titer screening (post-vaccination IgG levels) confirming immunity.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G+ spherical cells, grape-like clusters, non-motile, non-spore.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Aerobic/facultative anaerobe; smooth, convex colonies with golden (or white/lemon) pigment. Decomposes mannitol.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Strongest among non-spore bacteria; high salt tolerance (7.5% NaCl); resistant to drying; 90% penicillin-resistant.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Coagulase (clots plasma, limits lesions), SPA (binds Fc of IgG, anti-phagocytic), toxins (staphylolysin, leukocidin, exfoliative toxin, TSST-1, enterotoxin).

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Local pyogenic infections (furuncle, carbuncle, wound infection), systemic infections (bacteremia, osteomyelitis), toxin-mediated diseases (SSSS, TSS, food poisoning).

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Hygiene, drug sensitivity testing, penicillin-resistant penicillins (e.g., oxacillin) or vancomycin for MRSA.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G+ spherical cells, arranged in chains, capsulated in young cultures.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Facultative anaerobe, requires enriched media (blood agar); forms small colonies with a large zone of complete beta-hemolysis.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Weak; sensitive to normal disinfectants, heat, penicillin, and erythromycin.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: M protein (anti-phagocytic, cross-reacts with host tissue), lipoteichoic acid (adhesion), streptolysins (O & S), SK (streptokinase), SD (streptodornase), pyrogenic exotoxin (scarlet fever).

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Pyogenic infections (sore throat, tonsillitis, pyoderma, erysipelas, childbed fever), toxigenic diseases (scarlet fever), hypersensitivity diseases (acute glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever).

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Penicillin G is the absolute first choice; timely treatment of primary sore throat infection to prevent rheumatic fever.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G+ encapsulated lancet-shaped diplococcus in pairs.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Requires blood or serum; aerobic/facultative; displays alpha-hemolysis (green zone) on blood agar. Bile soluble (differentiates from S. viridans).

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Weak, highly sensitive to common disinfectants, heat, and optochin.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Capsule (main invasive power, inhibits phagocytosis), pneumolysin, neuraminidase.

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Lobar pneumonia (sharp pain, chills, fever, rusty sputum), meningitis, otitis media.

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Penicillin G, cephalosporins. Pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide vaccine available for high-risk individuals.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G- coffee bean or kidney-shaped diplococcus in pairs, possesses capsules and pili.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Aerobic; chocolate agar under 5%-10% CO2; autolytic enzymes make old cultures lyse quickly.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Very low; sensitive to cold, heat, drying, and disinfectants.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Capsule, pili (adhesion), strong Endotoxin (LPS, damages blood vessels, causes petechiae), IgA1 protease.

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Epidemic cerebrospinal meningitis (fever, headache, neck stiffness, skin petechiae, hemorrhagic rash).

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Penicillin G, ceftriaxone. Group-specific capsular polysaccharide vaccine used for prevention.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G- kidney-shaped diplococcus, coffee bean-shaped, typically found inside polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) in acute pus.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Aerobic; chocolate agar or Thayer-Martin medium under 5%-10% CO2.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Extremely weak; dies rapidly outside the human host; sensitive to cold and drying.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Pili (highly antigenically variable), outer membrane proteins, endotoxin (LPS), IgA1 protease. Destroys mucosal immunity.

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Gonorrhea (sexually transmitted urethritis, cervicitis with purulent discharge). Female infections are often asymptomatic early but can lead to PID. Neonatal ophthalmia (gonococcal conjunctivitis) via birth canal.

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Ceftriaxone or spectinomycin. Erythromycin eye drops for newborns. No vaccine due to high pilus variation.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G- short rods, mostly possess peritrichous flagella (motile) and pili (fecal-oral adhesion).

details.title: Culture
details.content: Aerobic/facultative; ferments lactose with gas (forms pink, large colonies on MacConkey/SS agar; green metallic sheen on EMB agar).

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Susceptible to heat and standard disinfectants; easily develops drug resistance via plasmid transfer.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Pili, enterotoxins (Heat-labile LT, Heat-stable ST), Shiga-like toxin, endotoxin, capsule.

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: UTI (most common cause), neonatal meningitis, septicemia. Gastroenteritis via pathotypes: ETEC (traveler's diarrhea), EPEC (infantile), EHEC (bloody diarrhea, HUS), EIEC (dysentery-like), EAggEC.

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Fluid/electrolyte management. Antibiotics (based on sensitivity test) for systemic infections. Hygiene.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G- short rods, possess pili for attachment, non-motile (no flagella).

details.title: Culture
details.content: Lactose non-fermenter; forms colorless, small, smooth colonies on SS agar.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Weak, highly sensitive to heat, drying, and gastric acid; S. sonnei is a late/slow lactose fermenter.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Pili (invasion of colonic epithelial cells), strong endotoxin (causes mucosal necrosis), Shiga exotoxin (Stx, enterotoxic, cytotoxic, neurotoxic).

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Bacillary dysentery (acute and chronic). Manifests as fever, abdominal pain, tenesmus, bloody purulent stools. Toxic megacolon/shock can occur.

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Oral rehydration, fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Strict personal hygiene. No widely used vaccine.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G- rods, possess peritrichous flagella (highly motile) and pili. Non-spore.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Lactose non-fermenter; forms colorless colonies with black centers (H2S production) on SS agar.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Moderate; easily killed by boiling (100°C) and standard pasteurization/disinfectants.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Invasion proteins (Vi antigen, anti-phagocytic), endotoxin, enterotoxin. Multiplies and survives inside macrophages.

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Enteric (Typhoid/Paratyphoid) fever (fever, rose spots, splenomegaly, leukopenia, intestinal hemorrhage/perforation in 3rd week), gastroenteritis, septicemia.

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Widal test for auxiliary diagnosis. Antibiotics (ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin). Typhoid vaccine (Vi polysaccharide) available.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G- comma-shaped curved rod, single polar flagellum ("shuttling like fish" darting motility).

details.title: Culture
details.content: Facultative anaerobe; grows in highly alkaline media (pH 8.5-9.5, alkaline peptone water); yellow colonies on TCBS agar.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Very weak; sensitive to heat, drying, and gastric acid; killed at 100°C in 2 minutes.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Flagella (penetrates mucus), pili (TCP, attachment), Cholera Toxin (exotoxin, activates adenylate cyclase -> high cAMP -> hypersecretion of water/electrolytes).

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Cholera (severe, painless watery diarrhea, "rice-water" stools, extreme dehydration, muscle cramps, hypovolemic shock).

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Immediate, massive oral/IV rehydration (essential), tetracycline/doxycycline to shorten shedding. Quarantine, sanitation.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G- polymorphic curved rod, halophilic (requires high salt, 3.5% NaCl).

details.title: Culture
details.content: Halophilic growth, green colonies on TCBS, Kanagawa phenomenon positive (produces thermostable direct hemolysin).

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Sensitive to heat, acid, and fresh water (dies in tap water).

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Thermostable direct hemolysin (TDH) and TDH-related hemolysin (TRH) (cytotoxic, cardiotoxic).

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Food poisoning (acute gastroenteritis with watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, fever) associated with raw/undercooked seafood.

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Self-limiting; hydration. Antibiotics only for severe cases.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G+ slender bacilli with terminal round spores, presenting a characteristic "drum-stick" appearance.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Obligate anaerobe, difficult to grow, swarming growth on blood agar.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Spores are extremely resistant; survive boiling for hours; killed only by autoclaving at 121°C under pressure.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Tetanospasmin (powerful neurotoxin, blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA/glycine -> continuous muscle contraction).

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Tetanus (lockjaw, trismus, spastic paralysis, opisthotonus, facial grimace/risus sardonicus). Wound must be anaerobic (deep/dirty).

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Wound debridement, Tetanus Antitoxin (TAT, must perform skin test first!), penicillin/metronidazole, DPT toxoid vaccine for prevention.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G+ large rectangular bacilli, non-motile, forms capsule in vivo, subterminal oval spore.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Anaerobic; produces "stormy fermentation" in milk medium (clots and gas) and double-zone hemolysis on blood agar.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Spores are highly resistant to heat, drying, and chemical disinfectants.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Alpha toxin (lecithinase, damages cell membranes, causes tissue necrosis and hemolysis), enterotoxin, theta toxin.

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Gas gangrene (myonecrosis, gas bubbles in tissue, foul odor, high mortality), food poisoning (watery diarrhea from reheated meat).

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Surgical debridement, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, high-dose penicillin G, gas gangrene polyvalent antitoxin.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: G+ bacilli, peritrichous flagella, subterminal oval spores ("tennis racket" shape).

details.title: Culture
details.content: Obligate anaerobe, grows on blood agar or cooked meat medium.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: Spores are extremely heat-resistant. However, the botulinum neurotoxin itself is heat-labile (destroyed by boiling for 10 min).

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Botulinum neurotoxin (the most potent poison known; blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions -> flaccid paralysis).

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Botulism (foodborne from canned foods: double vision, dysphagia, descending flaccid paralysis, respiratory failure). Infant botulism.

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Trivalent botulinum antitoxin, intensive respiratory support. Heat canned food thoroughly before consumption.

details.title: Morphology
details.content: Acid-fast positive thin, straight rods, waxy lipid-rich cell wall (mycolic acid), non-spore, non-motile.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Obligate aerobe; grows extremely slowly (doubling time 18 hrs); rough, wrinkled, off-white "bread crumb" colonies on Löwenstein-Jensen (L-J) medium in 2-4 weeks.

details.title: Resistance
details.content: High resistance to drying, acids, and alkalis (survives 3% HCl / 4% NaOH for 15 min); sensitive to wet heat (65°C 15min), alcohol (75%), and UV.

details.title: Pathogenesis
details.content: Intracellular survival in macrophages, lipids (cord factor, wax D, sulfatide, phospholipid) cause tissue necrosis and granuloma.

details.title: Clinical Findings
details.content: Tuberculosis: Primary TB (tubercles, caseous necrosis), Post-primary TB (secondary reactivation, lung cavities, chronic cough, bloody sputum), Miliary TB (disseminated).

details.title: Treatment & Prevention
details.content: Tuberculin skin test (PPD/OT) for diagnosis. BCG vaccine (live attenuated M. bovis) for infants. Multi-drug therapy (Isoniazid, Rifampin, Streptomycin).

details.title: Morphology
details.content: Acid-fast positive rods, typically arranged in bundles (globi) inside histiocytes.

details.title: Culture
details.content: Cannot be cultivated on artificial media or cell culture. Can only grow in armadillos or footpads of mice.

details.title: Resistance
